[L1] # SHIA-RAG: Semantic Hierarchy Induction Architecture for Retrieval-Augmented Generation
[L3] > Project Type: Minor Project (M.Tech)
[L4] > Date: August 2026
[L5] > Author: [Your Name]

[L9] ## Abstract
[L11] Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) has emerged as the dominant paradigm for grounding Large Language Model
(LLM) outputs in external knowledge. However, current RAG systems universally rely on flat text chunking — splitting
documents into fixed-size segments and retrieving the top-k most similar chunks. This approach destroys semantic continuity,
produces fragmented context, and fails at multi-hop reasoning.
[L13] We present SHIA-RAG (Semantic Hierarchy Induction Architecture for Retrieval-Augmented Generation), a novel 8-layer
RAG system that replaces flat chunks with a dynamically constructed Knowledge Forest — a collection of rooted trees where
each node represents a concept (with definitions, aliases, properties, and evidence) and edges encode hierarchical (IS_A,
PART_OF) and semantic (USES, CAUSES) relationships.
[L15] SHIA-RAG introduces five novel contributions: (1) Precedence-Constrained Tree Knapsack for context selection under
token budgets, ensuring hierarchical coherence; (2) Self-Evolving Knowledge Forest with a closed-loop feedback mechanism
that modifies edge weights based on retrieval success/failure; (3) Multi-Objective Energy Minimization for automated
hierarchy induction; (4) Adaptive Depth Traversal that adjusts retrieval depth based on query complexity; and (5) SHEF (SHIARAG Evaluation Framework), to the best of our knowledge, the first benchmark specifically designed for hierarchical RAG
quality.
[L17] The system processes raw documents through an offline pipeline (input → parsing → extraction → relation
management → hierarchy construction) and serves queries through an online pipeline (retrieval → generation with claim
verification). A continuous operations layer closes the feedback loop by updating the Knowledge Forest based on user
interactions.
[L19] Keywords: Retrieval-Augmented Generation, Knowledge Graph, Hierarchy Induction, Tree Knapsack, Self-Evolving
Knowledge Systems, Natural Language Processing

[L41] ## 1. Introduction
[L43] ### 1.1 Problem Statement
[L45] Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) has become the standard approach for grounding LLM outputs in external
knowledge. The typical RAG pipeline works as follows:
[L47] 1. Split documents into fixed-size text chunks (e.g., 512 tokens)
[L48] 2. Embed each chunk into a vector space
[L49] 3. At query time, retrieve the top-k most similar chunks
[L50] 4. Feed these chunks as context to an LLM for answer generation
[L52] While effective for simple factoid questions, this flat-chunk approach suffers from five fundamental limitations:
[L54] | Problem | Description | Impact |
[L55] |---------|-------------|--------|
[L56] | Broken semantic continuity | Fixed-size splits cut across paragraphs, definitions, and logical units | LLM receives
incomplete or incoherent context |
[L57] | Duplicate/fragmented information | The same concept may appear in multiple chunks with slight variations | Token
budget wasted on redundancy |
[L58] | Fixed granularity | All chunks are the same size regardless of content complexity | Cannot retrieve at different levels of
abstraction |
[L59] | Weak multi-hop reasoning | No explicit connections between chunks | Cannot follow reasoning chains (e.g., A → B →
C) |
[L60] | No cross-document fusion | Chunks from different documents are independent | Cannot merge knowledge from
multiple sources |
[L62] ### 1.2 Proposed Solution: SHIA-RAG
[L64] SHIA-RAG (Semantic Hierarchy Induction Architecture for Retrieval-Augmented Generation) addresses all five
limitations by replacing flat text chunks with a structured Knowledge Forest:
[L67] Traditional RAG:
[L68] SHIA-RAG:

Document → [Chunk₁, Chunk₂, ..., Chunkₙ] → Top-k → LLM
Document → Knowledge Forest (concepts + relations) → Adaptive Traversal → LLM

[L71] The system:
[L72] 1. Extracts knowledge — concepts, definitions, relations, and evidence from raw documents
[L73] 2. Builds a Knowledge Forest — a hierarchy of semantically linked concept nodes organized as rooted trees
[L74] 3. Retrieves knowledge nodes — by traversing the hierarchy (parents, children, cross-links) with adaptive depth

blob:https://chatgpt.com/22bc3c39-b594-46a2-bdf0-c46ad675ec43

2/597

03/09/2026, 14:49

[L75] 4. Selects context optimally — using a Tree Knapsack algorithm that respects hierarchical precedence constraints
[L76] 5. Generates verified answers — with claim-level evidence verification and citation binding
[L77] 6. Learns from feedback — a self-evolution loop that updates edge weights based on retrieval success/failure
[L79] > Key Insight: Humans organize knowledge by topics and subtopics (e.g., "Computer Science → Operating Systems →
Scheduling → Round Robin"), not by arbitrary text windows. SHIA-RAG mirrors this natural organization for AI retrieval.
[L81] ### 1.3 Objectives
[L83] 1. Design a complete 8-layer architecture for hierarchical RAG
[L84] 2. Define algorithms for automated hierarchy induction (CPG++, PRE, HV, FI, CLD)
[L85] 3. Implement a self-evolving feedback loop that improves retrieval quality over time
[L86] 4. Create a context selection algorithm that respects hierarchical constraints (Tree Knapsack)
[L87] 5. Develop an evaluation framework (SHEF) specifically for hierarchical RAG quality
[L88] 6. Provide a fully implementable specification with schemas, pseudocode, and deployment plans
[L90] ### 1.4 Contributions
[L92] This work makes five novel contributions to the RAG literature:
[L94] | # | Contribution | Novelty Level |
[L95] |---|-------------|---------------|
[L96] | 1 | Precedence-Constrained Tree Knapsack for context selection | Incremental (Novel Application) |
[L97] | 2 | Self-Evolving Knowledge Forest via retrieval feedback | Moderately Novel |
[L98] | 3 | Multi-Objective Energy Minimization for hierarchy induction | Moderately Novel |
[L99] | 4 | Adaptive Depth Traversal via query complexity classification | Incremental |
[L100] | 5 | SHEF — SHIA-RAG Evaluation Framework for hierarchical RAG | Incremental (Novel Combination) |

[L104] ## 2. Literature Review
[L106] ### 2.1 Related Work
[L108] #### 2.1.1 Flat-Chunk RAG Systems
[L110] The foundational RAG approach was introduced by Lewis et al. (2020), combining dense passage retrieval with seq2seq
generation. Subsequent systems — REALM (Guu et al., 2020), RETRO (Borgeaud et al., 2022), Atlas (Izacard et al., 2023), and
Self-RAG (Asai et al., 2024) — improved retrieval quality, generation faithfulness, and self-reflection, but all operate on flat
text chunks with no structural awareness.
[L112] #### 2.1.2 Structured RAG Systems
[L114] Recent work has begun exploring structured retrieval:
[L116] | System | Approach | Key Limitation |
[L117] |--------|----------|----------------|
[L118] | RAPTOR (Sarthi et al., 2024) | Recursive abstractive processing — clusters chunks and generates summaries at
multiple levels | Top-down summaries only; no concept-level extraction or entity resolution |
[L119] | GraphRAG (Edge et al., 2024) | Builds a knowledge graph from text, retrieves subgraphs | No hierarchy; flat graph
structure; no self-evolution |
[L120] | TreeRAG (Concept) | Organizes documents into topic trees for retrieval | No formal hierarchy induction algorithm;
manual tree construction |
[L121] | HiChunk (LlamaIndex) | Hierarchical chunking with parent-child relationships between chunks | Chunks are still text
fragments, not semantic concepts |
[L123] #### 2.1.3 Knowledge Graph Construction
[L125] Ontology learning and taxonomy induction have a rich history in NLP:
[L126] - Hearst patterns (Hearst, 1992) extract hypernym relations from text
[L127] - Taxonomy induction (Velardi et al., 2013; Bansal et al., 2014) builds hierarchies from web corpora

[L128] - Knowledge Graph Embedding (TransE, RotatE) learns vector representations of entities and relations
[L130] However, none of these systems integrate hierarchy construction with RAG retrieval and self-evolution.

[L161] ## 3. System Architecture
[L163] ### 3.1 Overview
[L165] SHIA-RAG is organized as an 8-layer pipeline divided into three phases:
[L167] | Phase | Layers | Mode | Purpose |
[L168] |-------|--------|------|---------|
[L169] | Phase 1: Offline | Layers 1-5 | Batch processing | Extract knowledge from documents and build the Knowledge Forest
|
[L170] | Phase 2: Online | Layers 6-7 | Real-time | Retrieve context and generate answers for user queries |
[L171] | Phase 3: Continuous | Layer 8 | Background | Monitor, collect feedback, and evolve the Knowledge Forest |
[L173] Additionally, Layer 0 is the foundational data model (schemas, types, database contracts) shared by all layers.

[L199] ### 3.2 Data Flow
[L202] Raw Document (PDF/DOCX/HTML)
[L203]
↓ Layer 1: Validate, detect format, extract text, OCR if needed
[L204] Normalized Text + Metadata
[L205]
↓ Layer 2: Detect layout, segment into blocks, classify types, reading order
[L206] [Page → Region → Block] hierarchy
[L207]
↓ Layer 3: Split sentences, extract concepts/definitions/relations
[L208] KnowledgeUnit objects (candidate concepts)
[L209]
↓ Layer 3: Alias resolution (merge synonyms via MinHash LSH)
[L210] KnowledgeNode objects (canonical, deduplicated)
[L211]
↓ Layer 4: Validate relations against ontology, score confidence
[L212] KnowledgeEdge objects (typed, scored)
[L213]
↓ Layer 5: CPG++ → PRE → HV → FI → CLD (hierarchy construction)
[L214] Knowledge Forest (rooted trees + cross-links)
[L215]
↓ Layer 6: Query → embed → find seeds → traverse → Tree Knapsack selection
[L216] Selected context nodes (within token budget)
[L217]
↓ Layer 7: Build prompt, invoke LLM
[L218]
↓ Layer 7: Verify claims against evidence, bind citations
[L219] Answer with citations + confidence score
[L220]
↓ Layer 8: Log, collect feedback, update forest weights

[L234] | 7 | Generation Engine | RetrievalResult | GenerationResult | Prompt assembly, claim verification |
[L235] | 8 | Operations | GenerationResult | Updated Forest | Feedback, self-evolution, monitoring |

Operating System manages computer resources.

Round Robin is a preemptive CPU scheduling algorithm.

Round Robin gives each process a fixed time quantum, for example 20 ms.

Round Robin is a type of CPU Scheduling Algorithm.

Round Robin uses Time Quantum.

Preemptive Scheduling contrasts with Non-Preemptive Scheduling.

Layer 0 – Data Model Foundation
You can explain it to your guide like this:
“Layer 0 is the foundation of the SHIA-RAG architecture. It does not process documents or retrieve information. Instead, it
defines how knowledge will be represented, connected, and validated throughout the entire system.”

The main idea
Layer 0 defines two core structures:
1. KnowledgeNode – represents a concept or piece of knowledge.
For example: Round Robin can be stored as a node with its name, definition, properties, evidence, confidence, and
embedding.
1. KnowledgeEdge – represents the relationship between two concepts.
For example:
Round Robin → IS_A → CPU Scheduling
Round Robin → USES → Time Quantum

It also defines

Types of relationships between concepts.
Rules to prevent invalid hierarchical structures, such as cycles.
Evidence and source tracking.
Confidence propagation rules.

[L193] ### 4.4 Confidence Propagation
[L194]
[L195] Node confidence is propagated from roots to leaves using **topological sort** (Kahn's algorithm) to guarantee
[L196]
[L197]

python
[L198] from collections import deque
[L199]
[L200] # Confidence weighting factors (must sum to 1.0)
[L201] ALPHA = 0.4 # Node's own extraction confidence weight
[L202] BETA = 0.4 # Parent confidence weight
[L203] GAMMA = 0.2 # Evidence confidence weight
[L204] DECAY = 0.95 # Per-level decay factor
[L205] BASE_CONFIDENCE = 0.5 # Default for root nodes (configurable)
[L206]
[L207] def propagate_confidence(forest):
[L208] """Propagate confidence scores from roots to leaves.
[L209]
[L210] Uses Kahn's algorithm (topological ordering) to ensure

blob:https://chatgpt.com/22bc3c39-b594-46a2-bdf0-c46ad675ec43

30/597

03/09/2026, 14:49

Layer Zero समझाना

[L211] parents are always processed before their children.
[L212] Processing in arbitrary order would give children stale
[L213] parent confidence values."""
[L214] in_degree = {n.id: len(forest.parents(n)) for n in forest.nodes()}
[L215] queue = deque([n for n in forest.nodes() if in_degree[n.id] == 0]) # Roots first
[L216]
[L217] while queue:
[L218] node = queue.popleft()
[L219] if forest.parents(node):
[L220] parent_confs = [p.confidence for p in forest.parents(node)]
[L221] avg_parent_conf = sum(parent_confs) / len(parent_confs)
[L222] evidence_conf = (
[L223] sum(e.confidence for e in node.evidence) / len(node.evidence)
[L224] if node.evidence else 0.5
[L225] )
[L226] node.confidence = (
[L227] ALPHA node.extraction_confidence +
[L228] BETA avg_parent_conf +
[L229] GAMMA evidence_conf
[L230] ) DECAY
[L231] else:
[L232] node.confidence = node.extraction_confidence or BASE_CONFIDENCE
[L233]
[L234] for child in forest.children(node):
[L235] in_degree[child.id] -= 1
[L236] if in_degree[child.id] == 0:
[L237] queue.append(child)
[L238]

[L332]
[L333] The parser uses rule-based heuristics for block classification:
[L334] - **Heading:** Short line (< 100 chars), no ending punctuation, starts with uppercase
[L335] - **List:** Starts with `- `, `* `, `• `, or `1.`
[L336] - **Table:** Contains 3+ pipe characters (`|`) — uses regex `re.match(r'^(def |class |import |from )', line)`
[L337] - **Code:** Uses regex pattern matching (NOT `"def " in text`, which falsely matches "definitely")
[L338] - **Definition:** Contains phrases like "is defined as", "refers to"
[L339] - **Default:** Paragraph
[L340]

[L696] --[L697]
[L698] ## Abstract
[L699]
[L700] Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) has emerged as the dominant paradigm for grounding Large Language Model
(LLM) outputs in external knowledge. However, current RAG systems universally rely on flat text chunking — splitting
documents into fixed-size segments and retrieving the top-k most similar chunks. This approach destroys semantic continuity,
produces fragmented context, and fails at multi-hop reasoning.
[L701]
[L702] We present SHIA-RAG (Semantic Hierarchy Induction Architecture for Retrieval-Augmented Generation), a novel 8layer RAG system that replaces flat chunks with a dynamically constructed Knowledge Forest — a collection of rooted trees
where each node represents a concept (with definitions, aliases, properties, and evidence) and edges encode hierarchical
(IS_A, PART_OF) and semantic (USES, CAUSES) relationships.
[L703]
[L704] SHIA-RAG introduces five novel contributions: (1) Precedence-Constrained Tree Knapsack for context selection under
token budgets, ensuring hierarchical coherence; (2) Self-Evolving Knowledge Forest with a closed-loop feedback mechanism
that modifies edge weights based on retrieval success/failure; (3) Multi-Objective Energy Minimization for automated
hierarchy induction; (4) Adaptive Depth Traversal that adjusts retrieval depth based on query complexity; and (5) SHEF (SHIARAG Evaluation Framework), to the best of our knowledge, the first benchmark specifically designed for hierarchical RAG
quality.
[L705]
[L706] The system processes raw documents through an offline pipeline (input → parsing → extraction → relation
management → hierarchy construction) and serves queries through an online pipeline (retrieval → generation with claim
verification). A continuous operations layer closes the feedback loop by updating the Knowledge Forest based on user
interactions.
[L707]
[L708] Keywords: Retrieval-Augmented Generation, Knowledge Graph, Hierarchy Induction, Tree Knapsack, Self-Evolving
Knowledge Systems, Natural Language Processing
[L709]

python
[L91] def needs_ocr(page) -> bool:
[L92] """Multi-signal OCR detection — more robust than text/area ratio alone.
[L93]
[L94] Signal 1: Text density (text chars / page area)
[L95] Signal 2: Font metadata availability (scanned pages lack font info)
[L96] Signal 3: Image coverage ratio (scanned pages are mostly images)
[L97] """
[L98] text = page.get_text()
[L99] area = page.rect.width page.rect.height
[L100]
[L101] # Signal 1: Text density
[L102] text_density = len(text.strip()) / max(area, 1)
[L103]
[L104] # Signal 2: Font metadata (scanned PDFs have no embedded fonts)
[L105] has_fonts = len(page.get_fonts()) > 0
[L106]
[L107] # Signal 3: Image coverage (scanned pages are large images)
[L108] images = page.get_images()
[L109] image_area = sum(img[2] img[3] for img in images) if images else 0
[L110] image_coverage = image_area / max(area, 1)
[L111]
[L112] # Decision: OCR needed if text is sparse AND (no fonts OR high image coverage)
[L113] if text_density < 0.1 and (not has_fonts or image_coverage > 0.5):
[L114] return True
[L115] return False

[L350] | CONFLICTING | Present both views with note |
[L351]

\overline{\text{claim\_conf}} + 0.2 \cdot \overline{\text{node\_conf}} + 0.1 \cdot \frac{|\text{cited nodes}|}{|\text{selected
nodes}|}$$

Signal 1 — Text Density
System check karta hai:
Text characters
────────────────
Page area

Agar text bahut kam hai → OCR ka possibility signal.

Signal 2 — Font Metadata
Normal digital PDF me embedded fonts ki information hoti hai.
Scanned PDF me generally:
Actual text = absent
Font information = absent

So system check karta hai:
Does the page have font metadata?

Signal 3 — Image Coverage
Scanned page usually ek large image hota hai.
System dekhta hai:
Page ka kitna area images cover kar rahi hain?

Decision roughly:
Text sparse?
AND
(No fonts OR high image coverage?)
│
▼
Use OCR

File me exactly ye three signals—text density, font metadata, aur image coverage—OCR decision ke liye use kiye gaye hain.
fileciteturn2file0L86-L116

Why is this better?
Single rule
↓
False detection ho sakti hai

❌

Multiple signals
↓
Better OCR decision ✓

17. Partial Extraction — Bahut important error handling
Real world me har PDF perfectly extract nahi hoti.
Maan lo:
100 pages total
95 pages → successfully extracted
5 pages → failed

System kya kare?
File ki policy:

Case 1: ≥ 80% pages successfully extract hue
Accept document ✓
partial_extraction = True
failed_pages = [...]

Case 2: < 80% pages successfully extract hue
Reject document ✗
Queue for manual review

Case 3: OCR confidence < 0.6
Document/page flag for manual review

File me ye best-effort policy explicitly defined hai. fileciteturn2file1L229-L237

Why 80% policy?
System do extreme approaches avoid karta hai:
Approach 1
1 page fail
↓
Reject entire 500-page document

Too strict ❌
Approach 2
90% pages fail
↓
Still accept

Too risky ❌
So:

21. Layer 1 ke possible errors aur safeguards
| Problem | Layer 1 ka response |
|---|---|
| Duplicate file | SHA-256 se detect, reject |
| Unsupported format | Validation me reject |
| Very large input | Size/page limits validate |
| Complex PDF | Fallback extraction path |
| Scanned PDF | OCR |
| Low text but not scanned | Multi-signal OCR detection |
| OCR mistakes | OCR confidence calculate |
| Low OCR confidence | Manual review flag |
| Some pages fail | Partial extraction policy |
| Too many pages fail | Reject + manual review |
| Repeated header/footer | Frequency-based safe removal |
| Language detection fails | English fallback |
Ye safeguards report ke Layer 1 implementation aur policies me defined hain. fileciteturn2file0L69-L116

|---|---|

Haan, bahut important question hai. Tumhara doubt valid hai:
“Jab document ka actual text already store ho raha hai, to metadata alag se kyu chahiye?”

Simple answer
Text batata hai document ke andar kya likha hai.
Metadata batata hai document kya hai aur kahan se aaya hai.

Hamara example
Maan lo document ka text hai:
Round Robin is a preemptive CPU scheduling algorithm.

Sirf text store karne se system ko ye pata chalega:
KYA likha hai?

✅

Lekin ye nahi pata chalega:

❌

Kis document se aaya?
Author kaun hai?
Document ka title kya hai?
Kab publish hua?

❌
❌

❌
Original file kaun si hai? ❌
Yahan metadata kaam aata hai.

Example
NormalizedDocument
│
├── Text
│
└── "Round Robin is a preemptive..."
│
└── Metadata
├── Title: Operating Systems

Layer 1 – Input Processing
You can explain it to your guide like this:
“Layer 1 is the entry point of the SHIA-RAG system. Its main purpose is to accept raw documents in different formats and
convert them into one clean and standardized format for the next layer.”

What happens in Layer 1?
Accepts documents such as PDF, DOCX, HTML, and TXT.
Checks whether the document is valid and not a duplicate using content hashing.
Extracts the text using format-specific tools.
If the document is scanned, it uses OCR to convert the image into text.
Checks the OCR confidence to identify unreliable extraction.
Cleans the extracted text and detects the document language.
Extracts basic metadata, such as title, author, and date.

Output
The final output is a NormalizedDocument, which contains:
Clean Text + Pages + Metadata + Language + OCR Information + Document Identity

This standardized document is then passed to Layer 2 for Document Parsing and Structure Identification.

Simple conclusion
“In short, Layer 1 acts as a quality and standardization gate. It converts different types of raw documents into a single,
reliable, machine-readable format so that all the next layers can process the document consistently.”

The supported formats, duplicate checking, extraction/OCR, confidence checks, cleaning, language detection, metadata, and
NormalizedDocument output are based on the Layer 1 specification in the uploaded SHIA-RAG report.

[L148]
[L149] The parser uses rule-based heuristics for block classification:
[L150] - **Heading:** Short line (< 100 chars), no ending punctuation, starts with uppercase
[L151] - **List:** Starts with `- `, `* `, `• `, or `1.`
[L152] - **Table:** Contains 3+ pipe characters (`|`) — uses regex `re.match(r'^(def |class |import |from )', line)`
[L153] - **Code:** Uses regex pattern matching (NOT `"def " in text`, which falsely matches "definitely")
[L154] - **Definition:** Contains phrases like "is defined as", "refers to"
[L155] - **Default:** Paragraph
[L156]

[L360] ### 3.1 Overview
[L361]

[L428]
[L429] The parser uses rule-based heuristics for block classification:
[L430] - **Heading:** Short line (< 100 chars), no ending punctuation, starts with uppercase
[L431] - **List:** Starts with `- `, `* `, `• `, or `1.`
[L432] - **Table:** Contains 3+ pipe characters (`|`) — uses regex `re.match(r'^(def |class |import |from )', line)`
[L433] - **Code:** Uses regex pattern matching (NOT `"def " in text`, which falsely matches "definitely")
[L434] - **Definition:** Contains phrases like "is defined as", "refers to"
[L435] - **Default:** Paragraph
[L436]

[L517]
[L518] ### 4.4 Confidence Propagation
[L519]
[L520] Node confidence is propagated from roots to leaves using **topological sort** (Kahn's algorithm) to guarantee
[L521]
[L522]

python
[L523] from collections import deque
[L524]
[L525] # Confidence weighting factors (must sum to 1.0)
[L526] ALPHA = 0.4 # Node's own extraction confidence weight
[L527] BETA = 0.4 # Parent confidence weight
[L528] GAMMA = 0.2 # Evidence confidence weight
[L529] DECAY = 0.95 # Per-level decay factor
[L530] BASE_CONFIDENCE = 0.5 # Default for root nodes (configurable)
[L531]
[L532] def propagate_confidence(forest):
[L533] """Propagate confidence scores from roots to leaves.
[L534]
[L535] Uses Kahn's algorithm (topological ordering) to ensure
[L536] parents are always processed before their children.
[L537] Processing in arbitrary order would give children stale
[L538] parent confidence values."""
[L539] in_degree = {n.id: len(forest.parents(n)) for n in forest.nodes()}
[L540] queue = deque([n for n in forest.nodes() if in_degree[n.id] == 0]) # Roots first
[L541]
[L542] while queue:
[L543] node = queue.popleft()
[L544] if forest.parents(node):
[L545] parent_confs = [p.confidence for p in forest.parents(node)]
[L546] avg_parent_conf = sum(parent_confs) / len(parent_confs)
[L547] evidence_conf = (
[L548] sum(e.confidence for e in node.evidence) / len(node.evidence)
[L549] if node.evidence else 0.5
[L550] )
[L551] node.confidence = (
[L552] ALPHA node.extraction_confidence +
[L553] BETA avg_parent_conf +
[L554] GAMMA evidence_conf
[L555] ) DECAY
[L556] else:
[L557] node.confidence = node.extraction_confidence or BASE_CONFIDENCE
[L558]
[L559] for child in forest.children(node):
[L560] in_degree[child.id] -= 1
[L561] if in_degree[child.id] == 0:
[L562] queue.append(child)
[L563]

[L73]
[L74] The parser uses rule-based heuristics for block classification:
[L75] - **Heading:** Short line (< 100 chars), no ending punctuation, starts with uppercase
[L76] - **List:** Starts with `- `, `* `, `• `, or `1.`
[L77] - **Table:** Contains 3+ pipe characters (`|`) — uses regex `re.match(r'^(def |class |import |from )', line)`
[L78] - **Code:** Uses regex pattern matching (NOT `"def " in text`, which falsely matches "definitely")
[L79] - **Definition:** Contains phrases like "is defined as", "refers to"
[L80] - **Default:** Paragraph
[L81]

[L411] def assign_reading_order(blocks: list) -> list:
[L412] """Assign global reading order with confidence.
[L413]
[L414] Multi-column layouts can produce incorrect reading order.
[L415] We detect potential issues and flag low confidence."""
[L416] # Sort by page, then y-coordinate, then x-coordinate
[L417] sorted_blocks = sorted(blocks, key=lambda b: (b.page_number, b.y_pos, b.x_pos))
[L418]
[L419] for i, block in enumerate(sorted_blocks):
[L420] block.reading_order = i
[L421]
[L422] # Detect potential multi-column issues
[L423] if i > 0:
[L424] prev = sorted_blocks[i - 1]
[L425] if (prev.page_number == block.page_number and
[L426] abs(prev.y_pos - block.y_pos) < 20 and # Same vertical band
[L427] prev.x_pos > block.x_pos): # But previous is to the right
[L428] block.confidence *= 0.7 # Reduce confidence — possible column issue
[L429]
[L430] return sorted_blocks

28. Final Summary
| Point | Layer 2 |
|---|---|
| Name | Document Parsing |
| Input | NormalizedDocument |
| Main purpose | Document ka structure understand karna |
| Hierarchy | Page → Region → Block |
| Main output | DocumentBlock[] |
| Block types | Heading, Paragraph, List, Table, Code, Algorithm, Definition, etc. |
| Main classification method | Rule-based heuristics |
| Code detection | Regex |
| Table parsing | pdfplumber + Camelot fallback |
| Reading order | Page → Top-to-Bottom → Left-to-Right |
| Quality check | Confidence scores |
| Next layer | Layer 3 — Knowledge Extraction |

Sabse important one-line understanding
“Layer 2 does not extract knowledge yet. It first converts the normalized document into structured blocks, identifies what each
block represents, and preserves the correct reading order. This structured output helps Layer 3 extract knowledge more
accurately.”

Layer 2 – Document Parsing
You can explain it to your guide like this:
“Layer 2 receives the NormalizedDocument from Layer 1 and understands the structure of the document. It does not extract
knowledge yet; instead, it identifies how the content is organized.”

What happens in Layer 2?
The document is organized into a Page → Region → Block structure.
Each region is divided into meaningful content blocks.
Every block is classified as a Heading, Paragraph, List, Table, Code, Algorithm, Definition, etc.
The system determines the correct reading order of the blocks.
Special structures such as tables and code are parsed separately when required.

Output
The final output is a list of DocumentBlock[] , where each block contains information such as:
Block Type + Text + Page Number + Region + Reading Order + Confidence

This structured output is then passed to Layer 3 for Knowledge Extraction.

Simple conclusion
“In short, Layer 2 converts a clean document into a structured representation. It tells the system what each part of the
document is and in what order it should be read, so that the next layer can extract knowledge more accurately.”

The explanation follows the file's Layer 2 structure of Page → Region → Block, block classification, reading order, special
structure parsing, and DocumentBlock[] output. fileciteturn6file0L42-L80

[L217] ## 13. Conclusion & Future Work
[L218]
[L219] ### 13.1 Summary
[L220]
[L221] This report presents SHIA-RAG, a novel 8-layer Retrieval-Augmented Generation system that replaces flat text chunks
with a dynamically constructed Knowledge Forest. The system introduces five novel contributions:
[L222]
[L223] 1. Precedence-Constrained Tree Knapsack — to the best of our knowledge, the first formulation of RAG context
selection as a precedence-constrained optimization problem
[L224] 2. Self-Evolving Knowledge Forest — to the best of our knowledge, the first closed-loop feedback mechanism that
modifies RAG knowledge structures based on retrieval success/failure
[L225] 3. Multi-Objective Energy Minimization — a formal optimization framework for automated hierarchy induction
combining semantic similarity, depth, confidence, and type coherence
[L226] 4. Adaptive Depth Traversal — query-complexity-aware retrieval depth adaptation for hierarchical RAG
[L227] 5. SHEF Evaluation Framework — to the best of our knowledge, the first benchmark specifically designed for
hierarchical RAG quality
[L228]
[L229] The complete system specification covers:
[L230] - 9 layers (Layer 0-8) with schemas, algorithms, pseudocode, and inter-layer data contracts
[L231] - 12 defined functions with complete implementations
[L232] - 12 relation types across 4 hierarchical and 8 semantic categories
[L233] - 8 schemas covering all data objects from document blocks to query logs
[L234] - A 6-month implementation roadmap with technology stack, folder structure, and CI/CD pipeline
[L235] - A comprehensive evaluation plan with datasets, baselines, ablation studies, and statistical significance testing
[L236]

[L371] #### Reading Order Validation
[L372]
[L373] Reading order is assigned left-to-right, top-to-bottom within each page. A confidence score tracks reliabilit
[L374]
[L375]

python
[L376] def assign_reading_order(blocks: list) -> list:
[L377] """Assign global reading order with confidence.
[L378]
[L379] Multi-column layouts can produce incorrect reading order.
[L380] We detect potential issues and flag low confidence."""
[L381] # Sort by page, then y-coordinate, then x-coordinate
[L382] sorted_blocks = sorted(blocks, key=lambda b: (b.page_number, b.y_pos, b.x_pos))
[L383]
[L384] for i, block in enumerate(sorted_blocks):
[L385] block.reading_order = i
[L386]
[L387] # Detect potential multi-column issues
[L388] if i > 0:
[L389] prev = sorted_blocks[i - 1]
[L390] if (prev.page_number == block.page_number and
[L391] abs(prev.y_pos - block.y_pos) < 20 and # Same vertical band
[L392] prev.x_pos > block.x_pos): # But previous is to the right
[L393] block.confidence *= 0.7 # Reduce confidence — possible column issue
[L394]
[L395] return sorted_blocks

[L76] #### Alias Resolution (with Antonym Protection)
[L77]
[L78] After extraction, multiple KnowledgeUnit objects may refer to the same concept (e.g., "RR", "Round Robin", "RoundRobin Scheduling"). Alias resolution merges them — but must avoid merging antonyms (e.g., "preemptive" and "nonpreemptive" have high similarity but are distinct concepts).
[L79]
[L80] 1. Build a MinHash LSH index (threshold=0.7) from concept names + aliases
[L81] 2. Antonym check: Before merging, verify candidates do not have a CONTRASTS_WITH relation
[L82] 3. Find connected components of near-duplicate units
[L83] 4. For each group: select canonical name (most frequent), merge all aliases, definitions, properties, and evidence
[L84]

[L87]
[L88]

"""Merge KnowledgeUnits referring to the same concept.

[L89]

Merge strategy:

[L90]
[L91]

- Canonical name: most frequent name across units
- Aliases: union of all names and aliases

[L92]
[L93]

- Definitions: union of all definitions
- Confidence: average of unit extraction confidences

[L94]

- Properties: merged (latest value wins, conflicts logged)

[L95]
[L96]

[L97]
[L98]

- Before merging, check if candidates have CONTRASTS_WITH relation
- Also check for negation prefixes (non-, un-, in-, dis-)

[L99]

[L101]

[L116]

[L117]
[L118]

[L119]

[L120]
[L121]

has_antonym = True

[L122]
[L123]

[L124]

[L125]
[L126]
[L127]
[L128]

# Don't merge

[L32] ### 5.4 Layer 4: Relation Management
[L33]
[L34] Responsibility: Validate candidate relations from Layer 3 against the relation ontology, score confidence, resolve crossdocument conflicts, and produce final KnowledgeEdge objects.
[L35]
[L36] Input: KnowledgeNode[] (with raw relations) → Output: KnowledgeEdge[] (validated, scored)
[L37]
[L38] Pipeline:
[L39] 1. Validate relation type — check against ontology; if unknown type, attempt inference via LLM
[L40] 2. Resolve target node — map target concept name to a KnowledgeNode
[L41] 3. Check for duplicates — merge evidence into existing edge if duplicate
[L42] 4. Determine edge class — hierarchical or semantic based on ontology mapping
[L43] 5. Calculate confidence — weighted combination of source confidence, evidence length, and semantic similarity
[L44] 6. Resolve cross-document conflicts — when multiple documents disagree on a relation
[L45]
[L46]
[L47] def calculate_edge_confidence(raw_rel, source, target) -> float:
[L48]

"""Confidence = 0.5 (base) + 0.15 * source_conf + 0.10 * evidence_quality + 0.10 * sim"""

[L49]
[L50]

conf = 0.5
conf += 0.15 * source.confidence

[L51]
[L52]

conf += 0.10 * min(len(raw_rel.get('evidence', '')) / 200, 1.0)
conf += 0.10 * cosine_similarity(source.embedding, embed(raw_rel['evidence']))

[L53]

return min(conf, 1.0)

[L56] #### Cross-Document Conflict Resolution
[L57]
[L58] When multiple documents provide conflicting relations for the same concept pair (e.g., Document A says "Round Robin
IS_A Scheduling" but Document B says "Round Robin PART_OF OS"), the system resolves conflicts using evidence-weighted

[L61] def resolve_cross_doc_conflicts(candidate_edges: list) -> KnowledgeEdge:
[L62]
"""Resolve conflicting relations from different documents.
[L63]
[L64]
[L65]

Strategy: Evidence-weighted voting
1. Group edges by (source_node, target_node) pair

[L66]
[L67]

2. For each group, tally votes per relation_type weighted by evidence confidence
3. Select the relation_type with highest weighted vote

[L68]

4. Log conflicts for manual review

[L69]
[L70]

"""
from collections import defaultdict

[L71]
[L72]

# Group by node pair

[L73]

pair_groups = defaultdict(list)

[L74]
[L75]

for edge in candidate_edges:
key = (edge.source_node, edge.target_node)

[L76]
[L77]

pair_groups[key].append(edge)

[L78]

resolved = []

[L79]
[L80]

for (src, tgt), edges in pair_groups.items():
if len(edges) == 1:

[L81]
[L82]

resolved.append(edges[0])
continue

[L83]
[L84]
[L85]

# Tally weighted votes per relation type
votes = defaultdict(float)

[L86]
[L87]

evidence_pool = defaultdict(list)
for edge in edges:

[L88]

weight = edge.confidence * len(edge.evidence)

[L89]
[L90]

votes[edge.relation_type] += weight
evidence_pool[edge.relation_type].extend(edge.evidence)

[L91]
[L92]

# Select winning relation type

[L93]

winner = max(votes, key=votes.get)

[L94]
[L95]

# Log conflict if close contest

[L96]
[L97]

sorted_votes = sorted(votes.items(), key=lambda x: x[1], reverse=True)
if len(sorted_votes) > 1:

[L98]

margin = sorted_votes[0][1] - sorted_votes[1][1]

[L99]
[L100]

if margin < 0.2: # Close contest
log_conflict(src, tgt, sorted_votes)

# Queue for manual review

[L101]
[L102]

winning_edge = edges[0]

[L103]

winning_edge.relation_type = winner

[L104]
[L105]

winning_edge.evidence = evidence_pool[winner]
winning_edge.confidence = calculate_edge_confidence_from_evidence(evidence_pool[winner])

[L106]
[L107]

winning_edge.metadata['conflict_resolved'] = True
winning_edge.metadata['alternative_relations'] = [

[L108]
[L109]
[L110]
[L111]
[L112]

(rt, score) for rt, score in sorted_votes if rt != winner
]
resolved.append(winning_edge)
return resolved

[L102] ### 3.1 Overview
[L103]
[L104] SHIA-RAG is organized as an 8-layer pipeline divided into three phases:
[L105]
[L106] | Phase | Layers | Mode | Purpose |
[L107] |-------|--------|------|---------|

[L109] | Phase 2: Online | Layers 6-7 | Real-time | Retrieve context and generate answers for user queries |
[L110] | Phase 3: Continuous | Layer 8 | Background | Monitor, collect feedback, and evolve the Knowledge Forest |

[L112] Additionally, Layer 0 is the foundational data model (schemas, types, database contracts) shared by all layers.

[L183]

[L184]
[L185]

- PARTIAL:
- UNSUPPORTED:

[L186]

[L189]
[L190]

[L193]
[L194]
[L195]
[L196]
[L197]

[L198]

[L199]
[L200]

[L201]

[L203]

[L204]
[L205]

return 'PARTIAL', avg_score

[L206]
[L207]

else:

[L210] #### Unsupported Claim Policy
[L211]
[L212] | Status | Action |
[L213] |--------|--------|
[L214] | SUPPORTED | Keep as-is with citation |

[L219] #### Answer Confidence Formula
[L220]
[L221] $$\text{confidence} = 0.4 \cdot \frac{\text{supported claims}}{\text{total claims}} + 0.3 \cdot
\overline{\text{claim\_conf}} + 0.2 \cdot \overline{\text{node\_conf}} + 0.1 \cdot \frac{|\text{cited nodes}|}{|\text{selected
nodes}|}$$

[L493] """Atomic unit of document structure."""

[L504]
[L505] The parser uses rule-based heuristics for block classification:
[L506] - **Heading:** Short line (< 100 chars), no ending punctuation, starts with uppercase
[L507] - **List:** Starts with `- `, `* `, `• `, or `1.`
[L508] - **Table:** Contains 3+ pipe characters (`|`) — uses regex `re.match(r'^(def |class |import |from )', line)`
[L509] - **Code:** Uses regex pattern matching (NOT `"def " in text`, which falsely matches "definitely")
[L510] - **Definition:** Contains phrases like "is defined as", "refers to"
[L511] - **Default:** Paragraph

[L553] --[L554]
[L555] ## 1. Introduction
[L556]
[L557] ### 1.1 Problem Statement
[L558]
[L559] Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) has become the standard approach for grounding LLM outputs in external
knowledge. The typical RAG pipeline works as follows:
[L560]
[L561] 1. Split documents into fixed-size text chunks (e.g., 512 tokens)
[L562] 2. Embed each chunk into a vector space
[L563] 3. At query time, retrieve the top-k most similar chunks
[L564] 4. Feed these chunks as context to an LLM for answer generation

blob:https://chatgpt.com/22bc3c39-b594-46a2-bdf0-c46ad675ec43

159/597

03/09/2026, 14:49

Layer Zero समझाना

[L565]
[L566] While effective for simple factoid questions, this flat-chunk approach suffers from five fundamental limitations:
[L567]
[L568] | Problem | Description | Impact |
[L569] |---------|-------------|--------|
[L570] | Broken semantic continuity | Fixed-size splits cut across paragraphs, definitions, and logical units | LLM receives
incomplete or incoherent context |
[L571] | Duplicate/fragmented information | The same concept may appear in multiple chunks with slight variations | Token
budget wasted on redundancy |
[L572] | Fixed granularity | All chunks are the same size regardless of content complexity | Cannot retrieve at different levels
of abstraction |
[L573] | Weak multi-hop reasoning | No explicit connections between chunks | Cannot follow reasoning chains (e.g., A → B →
C) |
[L574] | No cross-document fusion | Chunks from different documents are independent | Cannot merge knowledge from
multiple sources |
[L575]
[L576] ### 1.2 Proposed Solution: SHIA-RAG
[L577]
[L578] SHIA-RAG (Semantic Hierarchy Induction Architecture for Retrieval-Augmented Generation) addresses all five
limitations by replacing flat text chunks with a structured Knowledge Forest:
[L579]
[L580]
[L581] Traditional RAG:

Document → [Chunk₁, Chunk₂, ..., Chunkₙ] → Top-k → LLM

[L582] SHIA-RAG:
[L583]

Document → Knowledge Forest (concepts + relations) → Adaptive Traversal → LLM

[L584]
[L585] The system:
[L586] 1. Extracts knowledge — concepts, definitions, relations, and evidence from raw documents
[L587] 2. Builds a Knowledge Forest — a hierarchy of semantically linked concept nodes organized as rooted trees
[L588] 3. Retrieves knowledge nodes — by traversing the hierarchy (parents, children, cross-links) with adaptive depth
[L589] 4. Selects context optimally — using a Tree Knapsack algorithm that respects hierarchical precedence constraints
[L590] 5. Generates verified answers — with claim-level evidence verification and citation binding
[L591] 6. Learns from feedback — a self-evolution loop that updates edge weights based on retrieval success/failure

[L608] --[L609]
[L610] ## Abstract
[L611]
[L612] Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) has emerged as the dominant paradigm for grounding Large Language Model
(LLM) outputs in external knowledge. However, current RAG systems universally rely on flat text chunking — splitting
documents into fixed-size segments and retrieving the top-k most similar chunks. This approach destroys semantic continuity,
produces fragmented context, and fails at multi-hop reasoning.
[L613]
[L614] We present SHIA-RAG (Semantic Hierarchy Induction Architecture for Retrieval-Augmented Generation), a novel 8layer RAG system that replaces flat chunks with a dynamically constructed Knowledge Forest — a collection of rooted trees
where each node represents a concept (with definitions, aliases, properties, and evidence) and edges encode hierarchical
(IS_A, PART_OF) and semantic (USES, CAUSES) relationships.
[L615]
[L616] SHIA-RAG introduces five novel contributions: (1) Precedence-Constrained Tree Knapsack for context selection under
token budgets, ensuring hierarchical coherence; (2) Self-Evolving Knowledge Forest with a closed-loop feedback mechanism
that modifies edge weights based on retrieval success/failure; (3) Multi-Objective Energy Minimization for automated
hierarchy induction; (4) Adaptive Depth Traversal that adjusts retrieval depth based on query complexity; and (5) SHEF (SHIARAG Evaluation Framework), to the best of our knowledge, the first benchmark specifically designed for hierarchical RAG
quality.
[L617]
[L618] The system processes raw documents through an offline pipeline (input → parsing → extraction → relation
management → hierarchy construction) and serves queries through an online pipeline (retrieval → generation with claim
verification). A continuous operations layer closes the feedback loop by updating the Knowledge Forest based on user
interactions.
[L619]
[L620] Keywords: Retrieval-Augmented Generation, Knowledge Graph, Hierarchy Induction, Tree Knapsack, Self-Evolving
Knowledge Systems, Natural Language Processing

18. MinHash LSH ko simple language mein samjho
Suppose 1 million concepts hain.
Har concept ko har doosre concept se compare karna:
N × N comparisons

bahut expensive ho sakta hai.

↓

27. Layer 3 mein kaunsi technologies/algorithms use ho rahi hain?
| Technology / Algorithm | Kaam |
|---|---|
| LLM | Concepts, definitions, properties, candidate relations extract karna |
| Structured JSON output | Extracted knowledge ko standard format mein lena |
| Regex | Explicit definition patterns detect karna |
| Dependency Parsing | Grammatical definition structure detect karna |
| LLM fallback | Difficult definition classification |
| MinHash LSH | Similar aliases/duplicates efficiently find karna |
| Connected Components | Similar KnowledgeUnits ko groups mein organize karna |
| Antonym Protection | Opposite concepts ko galti se merge hone se bachana |
| Re-embedding | Merged canonical node ki fresh semantic representation banana |
Ye Layer 3 specification mein defined extraction, dependency-based definition detection, alias resolution, antonym
protection, aur re-embedding strategy se derived hai. fileciteturn8file0L20-L37 fileciteturn8file0L40-L74

| Point | Layer 3 |
|---|---|
| Name | Knowledge Extraction |
| Input | DocumentBlock[] |
| Main purpose | Structured blocks se actual knowledge extract karna |
| Extracts | Concepts, definitions, properties, candidate relations, domain |
| Intermediate output | KnowledgeUnit objects |
| Deduplication | Alias Resolution |
| Main algorithm | MinHash LSH |
| Special safeguard | Antonym Protection |
| Definition detection | Explicit patterns + Dependency Parsing + LLM fallback |
| Embedding after merge | Re-embed canonical node; don't average |
| Final output | Canonical, deduplicated KnowledgeNode[] |
| Next layer | Layer 4 — Relation Management |

Sabse important one-line understanding
“Layer 3 transforms structured document blocks into structured knowledge. It extracts concepts, definitions, properties, and
candidate relations, resolves different names of the same concept, and produces canonical, deduplicated KnowledgeNodes for
the next layer.”

Layer 3 – Knowledge Extraction
You can explain it to your guide like this:
“Layer 3 receives the structured DocumentBlock[] from Layer 2 and extracts actual knowledge from the document. It
identifies concepts, definitions, properties, and candidate relationships.”

What happens in Layer 3?
It extracts important concepts and technical terms.
It identifies definitions and properties related to those concepts.
It extracts possible relationships between concepts.
Different names of the same concept, such as “Round Robin” and “RR,” are identified and merged.
Finally, it creates clean and canonical KnowledgeNode[] objects while preserving the supporting evidence.

Output
Canonical KnowledgeNode[]

Each KnowledgeNode can contain:
Concept Name + Aliases + Definition + Properties + Evidence

This output is then sent to Layer 4, where the candidate relationships are validated and scored.

Simple conclusion
“In short, Layer 3 converts structured document content into actual, clean, and deduplicated knowledge that can be used to
build reliable relationships in the next layers.”

The explanation follows the Layer 3 source specification for concept, definition, property, candidate-relation extraction, alias
resolution, and canonical KnowledgeNode[] creation. fileciteturn8file0L14-L37 fileciteturn8file0L76-L99

[L53]
[L54] **Responsibility:** Validate candidate relations from Layer 3 against the relation ontology, score confidence,
[L55]
[L56] **Input:** `KnowledgeNode[]` (with raw relations) → **Output:** `KnowledgeEdge[]` (validated, scored)
[L57]
[L58] **Pipeline:**
[L59] 1. **Validate relation type** — check against ontology; if unknown type, attempt inference via LLM
[L60] 2. **Resolve target node** — map target concept name to a `KnowledgeNode`
[L61] 3. **Check for duplicates** — merge evidence into existing edge if duplicate
[L62] 4. **Determine edge class** — hierarchical or semantic based on ontology mapping
[L63] 5. **Calculate confidence** — weighted combination of source confidence, evidence length, and semantic similar
[L64] 6. **Resolve cross-document conflicts** — when multiple documents disagree on a relation
[L65]
[L66]

[L67] def calculate_edge_confidence(raw_rel, source, target) -> float:
[L68] """Confidence = 0.5 (base) + 0.15 source_conf + 0.10 evidence_quality + 0.10 sim"""
[L69] conf = 0.5
[L70] conf += 0.15 source.confidence
[L71] conf += 0.10 min(len(raw_rel.get('evidence', '')) / 200, 1.0)
[L72] conf += 0.10 cosine_similarity(source.embedding, embed(raw_rel['evidence']))
[L73] return min(conf, 1.0)

[L605] def calculate_edge_confidence(raw_rel, source, target) -> float:
[L606]

"""Confidence = 0.5 (base) + 0.15 * source_conf + 0.10 * evidence_quality + 0.10 * sim"""

[L607]

conf = 0.5

[L608]

conf += 0.15 * source.confidence

[L609]
[L610]

conf += 0.10 * min(len(raw_rel.get('evidence', '')) / 200, 1.0)
conf += 0.10 * cosine_similarity(source.embedding, embed(raw_rel['evidence']))

[L611]

return min(conf, 1.0)

[L18]
[L19] ## Abstract
[L20]
[L21] Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) has emerged as the dominant paradigm for grounding Large Language Model
(LLM) outputs in external knowledge. However, current RAG systems universally rely on flat text chunking — splitting
documents into fixed-size segments and retrieving the top-k most similar chunks. This approach destroys semantic continuity,
produces fragmented context, and fails at multi-hop reasoning.
[L22]
[L23] We present SHIA-RAG (Semantic Hierarchy Induction Architecture for Retrieval-Augmented Generation), a novel 8-layer
RAG system that replaces flat chunks with a dynamically constructed Knowledge Forest — a collection of rooted trees where
each node represents a concept (with definitions, aliases, properties, and evidence) and edges encode hierarchical (IS_A,
PART_OF) and semantic (USES, CAUSES) relationships.
[L24]
[L25] SHIA-RAG introduces five novel contributions: (1) Precedence-Constrained Tree Knapsack for context selection under
token budgets, ensuring hierarchical coherence; (2) Self-Evolving Knowledge Forest with a closed-loop feedback mechanism
that modifies edge weights based on retrieval success/failure; (3) Multi-Objective Energy Minimization for automated
hierarchy induction; (4) Adaptive Depth Traversal that adjusts retrieval depth based on query complexity; and (5) SHEF (SHIARAG Evaluation Framework), to the best of our knowledge, the first benchmark specifically designed for hierarchical RAG
quality.
[L26]
[L27] The system processes raw documents through an offline pipeline (input → parsing → extraction → relation
management → hierarchy construction) and serves queries through an online pipeline (retrieval → generation with claim
verification). A continuous operations layer closes the feedback loop by updating the Knowledge Forest based on user
interactions.
[L28]
[L29] Keywords: Retrieval-Augmented Generation, Knowledge Graph, Hierarchy Induction, Tree Knapsack, Self-Evolving
Knowledge Systems, Natural Language Processing
[L30]

[L53] ### 1.1 Problem Statement
[L54]
[L55] Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) has become the standard approach for grounding LLM outputs in external
knowledge. The typical RAG pipeline works as follows:
[L56]
[L57] 1. Split documents into fixed-size text chunks (e.g., 512 tokens)
[L58] 2. Embed each chunk into a vector space
[L59] 3. At query time, retrieve the top-k most similar chunks
[L60] 4. Feed these chunks as context to an LLM for answer generation
[L61]
[L62] While effective for simple factoid questions, this flat-chunk approach suffers from five fundamental limitations:

[L114] ### 5.4 Layer 4: Relation Management
[L115]
[L116] **Responsibility:** Validate candidate relations from Layer 3 against the relation ontology, score confidence
[L117]
[L118] **Input:** `KnowledgeNode[]` (with raw relations) → **Output:** `KnowledgeEdge[]` (validated, scored)
[L119]
[L120] **Pipeline:**
[L121] 1. **Validate relation type** — check against ontology; if unknown type, attempt inference via LLM
[L122] 2. **Resolve target node** — map target concept name to a `KnowledgeNode`
[L123] 3. **Check for duplicates** — merge evidence into existing edge if duplicate
[L124] 4. **Determine edge class** — hierarchical or semantic based on ontology mapping
[L125] 5. **Calculate confidence** — weighted combination of source confidence, evidence length, and semantic simila
[L126] 6. **Resolve cross-document conflicts** — when multiple documents disagree on a relation
[L127]

[L129] def calculate_edge_confidence(raw_rel, source, target) -> float:
[L130] """Confidence = 0.5 (base) + 0.15 source_conf + 0.10 evidence_quality + 0.10 sim"""
[L131] conf = 0.5
[L132] conf += 0.15 source.confidence
[L133] conf += 0.10 min(len(raw_rel.get('evidence', '')) / 200, 1.0)
[L134] conf += 0.10 cosine_similarity(source.embedding, embed(raw_rel['evidence']))
[L135] return min(conf, 1.0)

[L159] #### Alias Resolution (with Antonym Protection)
[L160]
[L161] After extraction, multiple KnowledgeUnit objects may refer to the same concept (e.g., "RR", "Round Robin", "RoundRobin Scheduling"). Alias resolution merges them — but must avoid merging antonyms (e.g., "preemptive" and "nonpreemptive" have high similarity but are distinct concepts).
[L162]

[L470] ### 2.1 Related Work
[L471]
[L472] #### 2.1.1 Flat-Chunk RAG Systems
[L473]
[L474] The foundational RAG approach was introduced by Lewis et al. (2020), combining dense passage retrieval with seq2seq
generation. Subsequent systems — REALM (Guu et al., 2020), RETRO (Borgeaud et al., 2022), Atlas (Izacard et al., 2023), and
Self-RAG (Asai et al., 2024) — improved retrieval quality, generation faithfulness, and self-reflection, but all operate on flat
text chunks with no structural awareness.
[L475]
[L476] #### 2.1.2 Structured RAG Systems
[L477]
[L478] Recent work has begun exploring structured retrieval:
[L479]
[L480] | System | Approach | Key Limitation |
[L481] |--------|----------|----------------|
[L482] | RAPTOR (Sarthi et al., 2024) | Recursive abstractive processing — clusters chunks and generates summaries at
multiple levels | Top-down summaries only; no concept-level extraction or entity resolution |
[L483] | GraphRAG (Edge et al., 2024) | Builds a knowledge graph from text, retrieves subgraphs | No hierarchy; flat graph
structure; no self-evolution |
[L484] | TreeRAG (Concept) | Organizes documents into topic trees for retrieval | No formal hierarchy induction algorithm;
manual tree construction |
[L485] | HiChunk (LlamaIndex) | Hierarchical chunking with parent-child relationships between chunks | Chunks are still text
fragments, not semantic concepts |
[L486]
[L487] #### 2.1.3 Knowledge Graph Construction
[L488]
[L489] Ontology learning and taxonomy induction have a rich history in NLP:
[L490] - Hearst patterns (Hearst, 1992) extract hypernym relations from text
[L491] - Taxonomy induction (Velardi et al., 2013; Bansal et al., 2014) builds hierarchies from web corpora
[L492] - Knowledge Graph Embedding (TransE, RotatE) learns vector representations of entities and relations
[L493]
[L494] However, none of these systems integrate hierarchy construction with RAG retrieval and self-evolution.
[L495]
[L496] ### 2.2 Research Gap

[L521] ## 3. System Architecture
[L522]
[L523] ### 3.1 Overview
[L524]
[L525] SHIA-RAG is organized as an 8-layer pipeline divided into three phases:
[L526]
[L527] | Phase | Layers | Mode | Purpose |
[L528] |-------|--------|------|---------|
[L529] | Phase 1: Offline | Layers 1-5 | Batch processing | Extract knowledge from documents and build the Knowledge Forest
|
[L530] | Phase 2: Online | Layers 6-7 | Real-time | Retrieve context and generate answers for user queries |
[L531] | Phase 3: Continuous | Layer 8 | Background | Monitor, collect feedback, and evolve the Knowledge Forest |
[L532]
[L533] Additionally, Layer 0 is the foundational data model (schemas, types, database contracts) shared by all layers.
[L534]

[L681] 3. Check for duplicates — merge evidence into existing edge if duplicate
[L682] 4. Determine edge class — hierarchical or semantic based on ontology mapping
[L683] 5. Calculate confidence — weighted combination of source confidence, evidence length, and semantic similarity
[L684] 6. Resolve cross-document conflicts — when multiple documents disagree on a relation

[L687] def calculate_edge_confidence(raw_rel, source, target) -> float:
[L688]
[L689]

"""Confidence = 0.5 (base) + 0.15 * source_conf + 0.10 * evidence_quality + 0.10 * sim"""
conf = 0.5

[L690]

conf += 0.15 * source.confidence

[L691]

conf += 0.10 * min(len(raw_rel.get('evidence', '')) / 200, 1.0)

[L692]

conf += 0.10 * cosine_similarity(source.embedding, embed(raw_rel['evidence']))

[L693]
[L694]

return min(conf, 1.0)

[L695]
[L696] #### Cross-Document Conflict Resolution
[L697]
[L698] When multiple documents provide conflicting relations for the same concept pair (e.g., Document A says "Round
Robin IS_A Scheduling" but Document B says "Round Robin PART_OF OS"), the system resolves conflicts using evidenceweighted voting:
[L699]
[L700] ```python
[L701] def resolve_cross_doc_conflicts(candidate_edges: list) -> KnowledgeEdge:
[L702] """Resolve conflicting relations from different documents.
[L703]
[L704] Strategy: Evidence-weighted voting
[L705] 1. Group edges by (source_node, target_node) pair
[L706] 2. For each group, tally votes per relation_type weighted by evidence confidence
[L707] 3. Select the relation_type with highest weighted vote
[L708] 4. Log conflicts for manual review
[L709] """
[L710] from collections import defaultdict
[L711]
[L712] # Group by node pair
[L713] pair_groups = defaultdict(list)
[L714] for edge in candidate_edges:
[L715] key = (edge.source_node, edge.target_node)
[L716] pair_groups[key].append(edge)
[L717]
[L718] resolved = []
[L719] for (src, tgt), edges in pair_groups.items():
[L720] if len(edges) == 1:
[L721] resolved.append(edges[0])
[L722] continue
[L723]
[L724] # Tally weighted votes per relation type
[L725] votes = defaultdict(float)
[L726] evidence_pool = defaultdict(list)
[L727] for edge in edges:
[L728] weight = edge.confidence * len(edge.evidence)
[L729] votes[edge.relation_type] += weight
[L730] evidence_pool[edge.relation_type].extend(edge.evidence)
[L731]
[L732] # Select winning relation type
[L733] winner = max(votes, key=votes.get)
[L734]

blob:https://chatgpt.com/22bc3c39-b594-46a2-bdf0-c46ad675ec43

220/597

03/09/2026, 14:49

Layer Zero समझाना

[L735] # Log conflict if close contest
[L736] sorted_votes = sorted(votes.items(), key=lambda x: x[1], reverse=True)
[L737] if len(sorted_votes) > 1:
[L738] margin = sorted_votes[0][1] - sorted_votes[1][1]
[L739] if margin < 0.2: # Close contest
[L740] log_conflict(src, tgt, sorted_votes) # Queue for manual review
[L741]
[L742] winning_edge = edges[0]
[L743] winning_edge.relation_type = winner
[L744] winning_edge.evidence = evidence_pool[winner]
[L745] winning_edge.confidence = calculate_edge_confidence_from_evidence(evidence_pool[winner])
[L746] winning_edge.metadata['conflict_resolved'] = True
[L747] winning_edge.metadata['alternative_relations'] = [
[L748] (rt, score) for rt, score in sorted_votes if rt != winner
[L749] ]
[L750] resolved.

[L78]
[L79] ### 4.2 KnowledgeEdge Schema
[L80]
[L81] Relationships between nodes are represented as `KnowledgeEdge` objects. There are **two edge classes**:
[L82]
[L83] | Edge Class | Structural Rule | Example |
[L84] |-----------|-----------------|---------|
[L85] | `HIERARCHICAL` | Must form an **acyclic forest** (single parent per node) | IS_A, PART_OF, SUBCLASS_OF, INST
[L86] | `SEMANTIC` | Unrestricted **graph** (cycles allowed) | USES, CAUSES, DEPENDS_ON, CONTRASTS_WITH, SIMILAR_TO
[L87]

[L251] ## 13. Conclusion & Future Work
[L252]
[L253] ### 13.1 Summary
[L254]
[L255] This report presents SHIA-RAG, a novel 8-layer Retrieval-Augmented Generation system that replaces flat text chunks
with a dynamically constructed Knowledge Forest. The system introduces five novel contributions:
[L256]
[L257] 1. Precedence-Constrained Tree Knapsack — to the best of our knowledge, the first formulation of RAG context
selection as a precedence-constrained optimization problem
[L258] 2. Self-Evolving Knowledge Forest — to the best of our knowledge, the first closed-loop feedback mechanism that
modifies RAG knowledge structures based on retrieval success/failure
[L259] 3. Multi-Objective Energy Minimization — a formal optimization framework for automated hierarchy induction
combining semantic similarity, depth, confidence, and type coherence
[L260] 4. Adaptive Depth Traversal — query-complexity-aware retrieval depth adaptation for hierarchical RAG
[L261] 5. SHEF Evaluation Framework — to the best of our knowledge, the first benchmark specifically designed for
hierarchical RAG quality
[L262]
[L263] The complete system specification covers:
[L264] - 9 layers (Layer 0-8) with schemas, algorithms, pseudocode, and inter-layer data contracts
[L265] - 12 defined functions with complete implementations
[L266] - 12 relation types across 4 hierarchical and 8 semantic categories
[L267] - 8 schemas covering all data objects from document blocks to query logs
[L268] - A 6-month implementation roadmap with technology stack, folder structure, and CI/CD pipeline
[L269] - A comprehensive evaluation plan with datasets, baselines, ablation studies, and statistical significance testing

[L293] --[L294]
[L295] ## Abstract
[L296]
[L297] Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) has emerged as the dominant paradigm for grounding Large Language Model
(LLM) outputs in external knowledge. However, current RAG systems universally rely on flat text chunking — splitting
documents into fixed-size segments and retrieving the top-k most similar chunks. This approach destroys semantic continuity,
produces fragmented context, and fails at multi-hop reasoning.
[L298]
[L299] We present SHIA-RAG (Semantic Hierarchy Induction Architecture for Retrieval-Augmented Generation), a novel 8layer RAG system that replaces flat chunks with a dynamically constructed Knowledge Forest — a collection of rooted trees
where each node represents a concept (with definitions, aliases, properties, and evidence) and edges encode hierarchical
(IS_A, PART_OF) and semantic (USES, CAUSES) relationships.
[L300]
[L301] SHIA-RAG introduces five novel contributions: (1) Precedence-Constrained Tree Knapsack for context selection under
token budgets, ensuring hierarchical coherence; (2) Self-Evolving Knowledge Forest with a closed-loop feedback mechanism
that modifies edge weights based on retrieval success/failure; (3) Multi-Objective Energy Minimization for automated
hierarchy induction; (4) Adaptive Depth Traversal that adjusts retrieval depth based on query complexity; and (5) SHEF (SHIARAG Evaluation Framework), to the best of our knowledge, the first benchmark specifically designed for hierarchical RAG
quality.
[L302]
[L303] The system processes raw documents through an offline pipeline (input → parsing → extraction → relation
management → hierarchy construction) and serves queries through an online pipeline (retrieval → generation with claim
verification). A continuous operations layer closes the feedback loop by updating the Knowledge Forest based on user
interactions.
[L304]
[L305] Keywords: Retrieval-Augmented Generation, Knowledge Graph, Hierarchy Induction, Tree Knapsack, Self-Evolving

[L329] ### 1.1 Problem Statement
[L330]
[L331] Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) has become the standard approach for grounding LLM outputs in external
knowledge. The typical RAG pipeline works as follows:
[L332]
[L333] 1. Split documents into fixed-size text chunks (e.g., 512 tokens)
[L334] 2. Embed each chunk into a vector space
[L335] 3. At query time, retrieve the top-k most similar chunks
[L336] 4. Feed these chunks as context to an LLM for answer generation
[L337]
[L338] While effective for simple factoid questions, this flat-chunk approach suffers from five fundamental limitations:

[L394]

[L471] Key design decisions:
[L472] - parent / children are convenience-only fields derived from hierarchical edges. In production, always derive these
from edge queries to avoid update anomalies (e.g., parent field says NODE_100 but the actual edge points to NODE_200 ).
These fields MUST NOT be treated as the source of truth.
[L473] - confidence is propagated from extraction confidence, parent confidence, and evidence confidence using topological
sort (see Section 4.4).
[L474] - abstraction_level (0.0 = very specific, 1.0 = very abstract) is used by CPG++ for parent filtering.
[L475] - extraction_confidence (not shown above) stores the original LLM extraction confidence before propagation. This is
the immutable baseline.
[L476]
[L477] ### 4.2 KnowledgeEdge Schema
[L478]
[L479] Relationships between nodes are represented as KnowledgeEdge objects. There are two edge classes:

Bilkul. Ab hum Layer 4 ko bhi same running example ke saath, step-by-step aur depth mein samjhenge.
Hum wahi example continue karte hain:
Operating Systems → CPU Scheduling → Round Robin → Time Quantum

Ab tak:
Layer 1 → Raw document ko clean kiya
Layer 2 → Document structure samjha
Layer 3 → Concepts aur candidate relations nikale
Layer 4 → Candidate relations ko validate karke reliable edges banayega

Layer 4 — Relation Management
Sabse pehle ek line mein samjho
Layer 4 receives KnowledgeNodes and the raw candidate relations extracted in Layer 3. It checks whether each relation is valid
according to the relation ontology, resolves the target concept, removes duplicates, calculates confidence, resolves conflicts
between documents, and creates final KnowledgeEdges.

Simple flow:
KnowledgeNode[]
(with candidate relations)
↓
Layer 4
↓
Validate Relation
↓
Resolve Source & Target
↓
Check Duplicate
↓
Determine Edge Class
↓
Calculate Confidence
↓
Resolve Document Conflicts
↓
Validated KnowledgeEdge[]
↓
Layer 5

Layer 4 ki exact responsibility hai candidate relations ko ontology ke against validate karna, confidence score karna, crossdocument conflicts resolve karna, aur final KnowledgeEdge objects banana. fileciteturn11file0L52-L74

6. Relation Ontology kya hoti hai?
Simple language mein:
Relation Ontology is a predefined set of allowed relationship types.

System kisi bhi random relation name ko graph mein add nahi karta.
Example:

❌ CONNECTS_TO_SOMETHING
❌ RELATED_IN_SOME_WAY
❌ UTILIZES_SOMEHOW
Instead, predefined relations use honge.

20. Evidence-Weighted Voting kya hai?
Suppose:
Round Robin → CPU Scheduling Algorithm

ke liye multiple documents relations suggest karte hain.
IS_A

Evidence:
Confidence = High
Evidence = Strong

PART_OF

Evidence:
Confidence = Low
Evidence = Weak

System simple vote counting nahi karti:
IS_A = 1
PART_OF = 1

Instead weight consider karti hai.
Source pseudocode mein weight:
weight =
edge.confidence × evidence length

Then:
Har relation type ka total weighted vote
↓
Highest vote wins

25. Layer 4 mein kaunsi technologies/algorithms use ho rahe hain?
| Technology / Method | Purpose |
|---|---|
| Relation Ontology | Allowed relation types validate karna |
| LLM Inference | Unknown relation type infer karna |
| Node Resolution | Target concept ko actual KnowledgeNode se map karna |
| Duplicate Detection | Same relation ki multiple edges avoid karna |
| Ontology Mapping | Hierarchical vs Semantic class decide karna |
| Cosine Similarity | Semantic evidence similarity measure karna |
| Confidence Scoring | Relation reliability score karna |
| Evidence-Weighted Voting | Cross-document conflicts resolve karna |
| Conflict Logging | Close conflicts ko manual review ke liye record karna |
Ye sab Layer 4 specification aur edge/ontology schema mein defined hain. fileciteturn12file8L676-L749
fileciteturn13file1L79-L129

26. Layer 4 mein possible errors aur safeguards
Error 1 — Invalid relation
Round Robin → RANDOM_RELATION → Time Quantum

Safeguard
Ontology Validation

Unknown relation ko direct accept nahi kiya jata; source design mein LLM-based inference attempt hota hai.

Round Robin
USES
Unknown Concept

Safeguard
Target Node Resolution

Relation ko actual KnowledgeNode se map karna zaroori hai.
Layer 0 edge validation mein missing source/target node ke liye explicit node-not-found errors bhi defined hain.

Round Robin → USES → Time Quantum

100 documents mein mil sakta hai.

Safeguard

+

hain. fileciteturn13file1L102-L129

27. Layer 4 kya nahi karti?
Ye samajhna bahut important hai.
Layer 4:
❌ Naye concepts primarily extract nahi karti
❌ Synonym/alias resolution nahi karti — ye Layer 3 ka main kaam tha
❌ Final hierarchy construct nahi karti
❌ Parent-child placement decide nahi karti
❌ Knowledge Forest nahi banati
Layer 4 ka main focus hai:
“Concepts ke beech extracted relationships ko validate, clean, score, and resolve karna.”

Actual hierarchy construction:
Layer 5

mein start hogi.

28. Layer 3 → Layer 4 → Layer 5 difference

LAYER 3
────────────────────────────
Knowledge Extraction
"Round Robin is a concept."
"RR is its alias."
"This is a possible relation."
↓
LAYER 4
────────────────────────────
Relation Management
"Is this relation valid?"
"Is it allowed by ontology?"
"Which actual nodes does it connect?"
"How confident are we?"
"Do documents disagree?"
↓
LAYER 5
────────────────────────────
Hierarchy Construction
"Where should this node be placed?"
"Who should be its parent?"
"Does the placement make sense?"
"Build the Knowledge Forest."

29. Real-world analogy
Imagine Layer 3 ek detective hai.
Detective kehta hai:
Mujhe evidence mila hai ki:
Round Robin
USES
Time Quantum

Lekin detective ka finding directly final court decision nahi hota.

Layer 4 ek verifier/judge ki tarah hai
Wo check karta hai:
✓ Is relation type valid?
✓ Kya dono concepts actually exist karte hain?
✓ Kya relation already known hai?
✓ Evidence kitna strong hai?
✓ Doosre documents kya bolte hain?
✓ Kya conflict hai?

Then final decision:
VALIDATED EDGE

Sabse important one-line understanding
“Layer 4 transforms the candidate relations extracted in Layer 3 into validated and reliable KnowledgeEdges by checking them
against a relation ontology, resolving the correct nodes, removing duplicates, calculating confidence, and resolving conflicts
between multiple documents.”

Complete flow yaad rakhne ke liye:
Candidate Relation
↓
Ontology Validation
↓
Node Resolution
↓
Duplicate Check
↓
Edge Classification
↓
Confidence Scoring
↓
Conflict Resolution
↓
Validated KnowledgeEdge
↓
LAYER 5

Sabse important conceptual shift:
Layer 3 says: “I found a possible connection.”
Layer 4 says: “I have validated, scored, and structured this connection so the system can safely use it.”

C H ATG P T 24/08/2026, 00:36:28

Layer 4 – Relation Management
You can explain it to your guide like this:
“Layer 4 receives the candidate relationships extracted in Layer 3 and verifies whether those relationships are correct and
reliable. It checks each relation against a predefined relation ontology, connects it to the correct KnowledgeNodes, removes
duplicates, calculates a confidence score, and handles conflicts between different documents.”

What happens in Layer 4?

blob:https://chatgpt.com/22bc3c39-b594-46a2-bdf0-c46ad675ec43

257/597

03/09/2026, 14:49

Layer Zero समझाना

It validates the relation type, such as IS_A , PART_OF , or USES .
It maps the relation to the correct source and target KnowledgeNodes.
It removes duplicate relationships and combines their evidence.
It classifies relations as Hierarchical or Semantic.
It calculates a confidence score based on the source and evidence quality.
If multiple documents provide conflicting relations, it resolves the conflict using the available evidence.

Example
Layer 3:
Round Robin → USES → Time Quantum
↓
Layer 4:
Validate + Check Evidence + Calculate Confidence
↓
Final KnowledgeEdge

Output
KnowledgeEdge[]

Simple conclusion
“In short, Layer 4 acts as a quality-control layer for relationships. It ensures that only valid, reliable, and well-supported
connections between knowledge concepts are passed to the next layer for hierarchy construction.”

[L537] ### 4.3 Tree vs DAG vs Graph
[L538]
[L539] | PDF | Claim |
[L540] |-----|-------|
[L541] | All PDFs | "Knowledge Forest is acyclic (no loops)" |
[L542] | All PDFs | "Cross-Link Discovery (CLD) adds semantic associations" |
[L543]
[L544] Contradiction: Cross-links create graph cycles. The forest is only acyclic in its hierarchical edges (parent-child). Crosslinks form a separate semantic graph layer.
[L545]
[L546] Resolution: Define two distinct edge types:
[L547] 1. Hierarchical edges (IS_A, PART_OF) — must be acyclic, form a forest
[L548] 2. Semantic edges (USES, RELATED_TO, CAUSES) — may form cycles, separate graph layer
[L549]
[L550] > [!IMPORTANT]
[L551] > Single-Parent Constraint: SHIA-RAG enforces strict single-parent trees for hierarchical edges. Each node has at
most one parent in the hierarchy. DAG support (multiple parents) is deferred to future work. This simplifies:
[L552] > - Precedence constraints in Tree Knapsack: $x_i \leq x_{\text{parent}(i)}$ is unambiguous
[L553] > - Confidence propagation: single parent path, no need for multi-parent averaging
[L554] > - Cycle detection: simple ancestor traversal
[L555] >
[L556] > Multiple semantic associations are handled via SEMANTIC edges (cross-links), which are unrestricted.
[L557]
[L558]

blob:https://chatgpt.com/22bc3c39-b594-46a2-bdf0-c46ad675ec43

269/597

03/09/2026, 14:49

Layer Zero समझाना

[L559] # Explicit enforcement of single-parent constraint

existing_parents = [

[L573] --[L574]
[L575] ## 5. Novelty Contributions
[L576]
[L577] > [!IMPORTANT]
[L578] > These are 5 novel contributions that make SHIA-RAG publishable and distinguish it from all existing RAG systems
(TreeRAG, HiChunk, RAPTOR, GraphRAG, etc.).
[L579]
[L580] ### Novelty 1: Precedence-Constrained Tree Knapsack for Context Selection
[L581]
[L582] What exists: All current RAG systems use flat top-k selection or simple greedy knapsack for context packing.
[L583]
[L584] What SHIA-RAG proposes: A greedy approximation for the Tree Knapsack formulation where selecting a child node
forces inclusion of its parent (precedence constraint). This ensures hierarchical coherence in the assembled context.
[L585]
[L586] $$\max \sum_{i=1}^{n} U_i \cdot x_i \quad \text{s.t.} \quad \sum_{i=1}^{n} C_i \cdot x_i \leq B, \quad x_i \leq
x_{\text{parent}(i)} \quad \forall i$$
[L587]
[L588] > [!NOTE]
[L589] > The implementation uses a greedy utility-density heuristic rather than exact DP, as exact solutions are
computationally prohibitive for large token budgets. The precedence-constrained formulation itself is the novelty.
[L590]
[L591] Why novel: No RAG paper has formulated context selection as a precedence-constrained optimization problem. The
adaptation of the Tree Knapsack formulation from operations research to RAG context selection is a direct, citable
contribution (incremental but novel application).
[L592]
[L593] --[L594]
[L595] ### Novelty 2: Self-Evolving Knowledge Forest via Retrieval Feedback
[L596]
[L597] What exists: All current Knowledge Graphs and hierarchies are static after construction.

[L662] If both agents produce the same response in any round,
[L663] the debate terminates early with a consensus, considering
[L664] predefined thresholds of the stability score. Otherwise, the
[L665] current round is appended to the debate history. If consensus
[L666] is not reached or the responses fall below the thresholds
[L667] for faithfulness or answer relevance, the debate continues
[L668] until round T. The Judge agent AJ then determines the final
[L669] outcome.
[L670] Judge Decision(triggered only when the debate reaches
[L671] the final round) If the agents fail to reach a consensus by the
[L672] final round T, the Judge agent AJ makes the final decision
[L673] based on the original claim c, the complete debate history
[L674] H, and the stability score S. Here, S is composed of the
[L675] average faithfulness and answer relevance scores across all
[L676] rounds, capturing the overall quality of the agents’ responses.
[L677] This decision process is formalized as:
[L678] f inal answer = Judge(AJ , H, S, c) (7)
[L679] The LLM-based Judge agent receives the stability score S
[L680] and debate history H as part of its prompt and makes the final
[L681] decision by jointly considering both.
[L682] For reproducibility, we provide the full prompts used for
[L683] the debate round, query selection, and judge components in
[L684] Figures 4, 5, and 6. Note that the prompt for the initial
[L685] round corresponds to the same template with the opponent’s
[L686] response removed.

[L266] ### 7. Hierarchy Construction (SHIA Core)
[L267] Input: Canonical KnowledgeNodes and accepted relations (from KCE).
[L268] Output: A Knowledge Forest: one or more concept trees (plus sibling links).
[L269]
[L270] Goal: For each node, determine the best parent(s) and place it in the forest. This is done incrementally for all nodes.

blob:https://chatgpt.com/22bc3c39-b594-46a2-bdf0-c46ad675ec43

279/597

03/09/2026, 14:49

Layer Zero समझाना

We formalize SHIA as the following sub-algorithms:
[L271]
[L272] - Candidate Parent Generation (CPG++): Given a node n, quickly identify a small set of plausible parent nodes from the
forest.
[L273] - Parent Ranking Engine (PRE): Score each candidate parent using multiple signals (semantic similarity, hypernym
patterns, evidence support, generality) and pick the best.
[L274] - Hierarchy Validation (HV): Verify that adding n under the chosen parent does not create cycles, exceed depth limits,
or violate sibling coherence.
[L275] - Forest Integration (FI): Attach n to the forest under its parent (or create new tree if no parent).
[L276] - Cross-Link Discovery (CLD): Add additional “soft links” between nodes (e.g. semantic associations) that do not form
the main parent-child tree but could aid retrieval.
[L277]
[L278] We describe each in detail below.
[L279]
[L280] #### 7.1 Candidate Parent Generation (CPG++)
[L281] Challenge: The forest may contain tens of thousands of nodes (all concepts from the corpus). A naive linear search for
a parent is infeasible.
[L282]
[L283] Solution: CPG++ is a multi-stage hypothesis generator that dramatically prunes the search space. For a new or existing
node q, it performs:
[L284] 1. Domain Routing: Use document metadata or concept taxonomy (if available) to narrow candidate domains. For
example, if q came from an OS textbook, restrict to OS-related nodes. Domain labels (from ontology or section context) filter
the forest.
[L285] 2. ANN Retrieval: Use a vector index (e.g. HNSW) over node embeddings. Query q’s embedding to retrieve top-𝑘
nearest existing nodes (𝑘 ≈ 20–50). This runs in ≈O(log N) time.
[L286] 3. Relation Filter: From the top-𝑘 neighbors, keep only those with some plausible relation. For instance, if q is a
“Scheduling” algorithm, neighbors like “Process” or “Operating System” might pass (if relations exist), while unrelated ones
are dropped. We may use the relation set or co-occurrence stats: e.g. keep neighbor p only if LLM suggests a relation q→p (isa/part-of) or vice versa.
[L287] 4. Abstraction Filter: Estimate abstraction levels. Compute a genericity score for each candidate (e.g. children count or
learned metric). Reject candidates that are too abstract or too specific. For example, if q=“Round Robin”, reject “Operating
System” (too high) and “Time Quantum” (too low) at this stage.
[L288] 5. Evidence Filter: Optionally, verify candidates against cross-document evidence. If multiple sources have already
related q to c, boost score; if none, deprioritize.
[L289]
[L290] The output is a small candidate set (e.g. ≤5 hypotheses), each with initial scores or confidence. CPG++ never declares
the single parent; it only proposes plausible parents for PRE to rank.
