[L300] document_chunk_id: file_00000000f54081fa942542456259658a--1--13
[L301] snippet:
[L302] Using either rule-based extraction (Hearst patterns for hypernymy) or LLM prompts, we refine relations:
[L303] - Hypernym (is-a): Identify “X is a type of Y”. Mark X→Y “is-a”.
[L304] - Part-of / Contains: “X consists of Y”.
[L305] - Cause-effect, uses, synonyms, etc. The main goal is to detect parent-child or sibling-type edges.
[L306] - Relations may be directed with types. Each edge gets a confidence (LLM-provided probability or similarity score).
[L307]
[L308] We aggregate relation mentions from all documents. If multiple sources assert the same relation, confidence
increases.
[L309]
[L310] API: detect_relations(concept) -> list of (relation, target_concept, confidence) .
[L311]
[L312] Data: We update nodes: e.g. node “Round Robin” gains a “is-a → CPU Scheduling” relation.
[L313]
[L314] ### 6. Knowledge Confidence Engine (KCE)
[L315] Input: All extracted relations and definitions with confidence estimates.
[L316] Output: Filtered set of reliable relations for hierarchy building; uncertain cases flagged or queued for review.
[L317]
[L318] To prevent “garbage in” from corrupting the structure, we apply thresholds:
[L319] - If confidence ≥ high_threshold (e.g. 0.9), accept relation automatically.
[L320] - If confidence in [low, high), mark as pending for later re-evaluation.
[L321] - If below low_threshold (e.g. <0.5), reject or set aside.
[L322]
[L323] We also check consistency: conflicting high-confidence relations (e.g. A is-a B and A is-a C where B≠C) are flagged.
[L324]
[L325] Pseudocode (KCE):
[L326]
[L327] for each relation r in all_relations:
[L328]
[L329]

if r.confidence >= HIGH:
accepted_relations.add(r)

[L330]

else if r.confidence >= LOW:

[L331]
[L332]
[L333]
[L334]

pending_relations.add(r)
else:
reject r

[L335] Nodes carry a confidence score based on their sources. Relations are stored with these labels.
[L336]
[L337] At runtime, pending relations can be confirmed by consensus (e.g. multiple docs) or via user review.
[L338]
[L339] ### 7. Hierarchy Construction (SHIA Core)
[L340] Input: Canonical KnowledgeNodes and accepted relations (from KCE).
[L341] Output: A Knowledge Forest: one or more concept trees (plus sibling links).
[L342]
[L343] Goal: For each node, determine the best parent(s) and place it in the forest. This is done incrementally for all nodes.
We formalize SHIA as the following sub-algorithms:
[L344]
[L345] - Candidate Parent Generation (CPG++): Given a node n, quickly identify a small set of plausible parent nodes from the
forest.
[L346] - Parent Ranking Engine (PRE): Score each candidate parent using multiple signals (semantic similarity, hypernym

blob:https://chatgpt.com/22bc3c39-b594-46a2-bdf0-c46ad675ec43

281/597

03/09/2026, 14:49

Layer Zero समझाना

patterns, evidence support, generality) and pick the best.
[L347] - Hierarchy Validation (HV): Verify that adding n under the chosen parent does not create cycles, exceed depth limits,
or violate sibling coherence.
[L348] - Forest Integration (FI): Attach n to the forest under its parent (or create new tree if no parent).
[L349] - Cross-Link Discovery (CLD): Add additional “soft links” between nodes (e.g. semantic associations) that do not form
the main parent-child tree but could aid retrieval.
[L350]
[L351] We describe each in detail below.
[L352]
[L353] #### 7.1 Candidate Parent Generation (CPG++)
[L354] Challenge: The forest may contain tens of thousands of nodes (all concepts from the corpus). A naive linear search for
a parent is infeasible.
[L355]
[L356] Solution: CPG++ is a multi-stage hypothesis generator that dramatically prunes the search space.

[L792] def cpg_plus_plus(node_q, forest, config):
[L793]

"""Generate ≤k candidate parents for node q."""

[L794]
[L795]

# Stage 1: Domain Routing (O(1)) — filter to same-domain nodes
domain = classify_domain(node_q)

[L796]

domain_nodes = forest.get_nodes_by_domain(domain)

[L797]
[L798]

# Stage 2: ANN Retrieval (O(log N)) — find semantically similar nodes

[L799]
[L800]

if len(domain_nodes) > config.ann_k:
ann_results = vector_index.search(node_q.embedding, k=config.ann_k)

[L801]
[L802]

candidates = [r for r in ann_results if r in domain_nodes]
else:

[L803]

candidates = domain_nodes

[L804]
[L805]

# Stage 3: Relation Filter — keep only nodes with plausible relations

[L806]

candidates = [c for c in candidates if has_plausible_relation(node_q, c)]

[L807]
[L808]

# Stage 4: Abstraction Filter — parent must be MORE abstract

[L809]
[L810]

q_level = estimate_abstraction_level(node_q)
candidates = [c for c in candidates

[L811]

if c.abstraction_level > q_level

[L812]

and abs(q_level - c.abstraction_level) < config.max_level_gap]

[L813]
[L814]
[L815]

# Stage 5: Evidence Filter — prioritize cross-document evidence
candidates = sorted(candidates,

[L816]

key=lambda c: cross_doc_evidence_count(node_q, c), reverse=True)

[L817]
[L818]

return candidates[:config.max_candidates]

# Return top 5

[L283] def calculate_edge_confidence(raw_rel, source, target) -> float:
[L284]
"""Confidence = 0.5 (base) + 0.15 * source_conf + 0.10 * evidence_quality + 0.10 * sim"""
[L285]

conf = 0.5

[L286]

conf += 0.15 * source.confidence

[L287]

conf += 0.10 * min(len(raw_rel.get('evidence', '')) / 200, 1.0)

[L288]
[L289]

conf += 0.10 * cosine_similarity(source.embedding, embed(raw_rel['evidence']))
return min(conf, 1.0)

[L334]

[L336]

[L376] #### 5.5.2 PRE — Parent Ranking Engine

[L378] Ranks all candidates using a weighted scoring formula:
[L379]
[L380] $$\text{Score}(P, N) = w_1 \cdot \cos(E_P, E_N) + w_2 \cdot H(P, N) + w_3 \cdot \frac{D_{\max} - \text{depth}
[L381]
[L382] Where:
[L383] - $w_1=0.30$ — Embedding cosine similarity
[L384] - $w_2=0.25$ — Hypernym score (Hearst patterns + LLM fallback)
[L385] - $w_3=0.15$ — Depth penalty (shallower parents preferred; $D_{\max}=8$)
[L386] - $w_4=0.20$ — Evidence support

Layer Zero समझाना

Hum wahi example continue karenge:
Operating Systems → CPU Scheduling → CPU Scheduling Algorithm → Round Robin → Time Quantum

Layer 5 — SHIA Core / Hierarchy Construction
Sabse pehle ek line mein samjho
Layer 5 takes the validated KnowledgeNodes and KnowledgeEdges from the previous layers and decides where each concept
should be placed inside the Knowledge Forest.

Simple words mein:
Layer 3 ne concepts banaye.

Layer 4 ne unke relations validate kiye.

Layer 5 decide karta hai: “Kaunsa concept kis concept ke under jaana chahiye?”

File ke according Layer 5 ka input KnowledgeNode[] + KnowledgeEdge[] hai aur output Knowledge Forest hai. Iske five main
components hain: CPG++ → PRE → HV → FI → CLD. fileciteturn15file0L23-L44

1. Layer 5 ki zarurat kyu padi?
Layer 4 ke baad maan lo hamare paas ye nodes hain:
Operating Systems
CPU Scheduling
CPU Scheduling Algorithm
Round Robin
Time Quantum

Aur relations hain:
Round Robin
IS_A
CPU Scheduling Algorithm
Round Robin
USES
Time Quantum

Ab problem:

System ko abhi ye nahi pata ki final hierarchy kya hogi
For example:

blob:https://chatgpt.com/22bc3c39-b594-46a2-bdf0-c46ad675ec43

309/597

03/09/2026, 14:49

Layer Zero समझाना

Operating Systems
│
▼
CPU Scheduling
│
▼
CPU Scheduling Algorithm
│
▼
Round Robin

Ye structure automatically sirf concepts aur relations se final form mein ready nahi hota.
System ko decide karna padega:
Round Robin ka parent kaun hoga?
CPU Scheduling?
CPU Scheduling Algorithm?
Operating Systems?
Kya Round Robin ek new root hona chahiye?
Kya hierarchy mein cycle ban rahi hai?
Kya Time Quantum ko parent banana chahiye? ❌
Kya USES relation ko hierarchy mein convert karna chahiye? ❌

Layer 5 ye sab decisions leta hai.

2. Layer 5 ka main goal
Har new concept ke liye:
New Node
↓
Possible parents find karo
↓
Best parent choose karo
↓
Check karo placement valid hai ya nahi
↓
Forest mein insert karo
↓
Additional semantic connections discover karo

So overall:
KnowledgeNodes + KnowledgeEdges
↓
Layer 5 – SHIA Core
↓

| HV | Depth Constraint | Tree excessively deep na ho |
| HV | Sibling Coherence | Related concepts ko coherent siblings banana |
| FI | Tree Insertion | Node ko forest mein place karna |
| CLD | ANN + Similarity Threshold | Semantic cross-links discover karna |
| Storage | Graph DB + Vector DB | Forest aur embeddings store/retrieve karna |
The report describes ANN indexes such as HNSW and examples like FAISS/Qdrant, along with graph/in-memory structures for
the forest. fileciteturn16file3L259-L269

40. Layer 5 mein possible errors aur safeguards
Error 1 — Wrong parent select hona
Example:
Round Robin
↓
Operating System

Jab better parent:
CPU Scheduling Algorithm

ho.

Safeguard
CPG++
↓
PRE Multi-Signal Ranking

Error 2 — Semantic relation ko hierarchy bana dena
Example:
Round Robin
USES
Time Quantum

Galat:
Round Robin
↓
Time Quantum

as parent-child.

Safeguard
Hierarchical aur semantic edges ko separate classes mein maintain kiya jata hai. fileciteturn14file7L544-L556

Error 3 — Cycle ban jana
A → B → C
↑
│
└───────┘

Safeguard

Error 4 — Multiple parents
Example:
A
↙
Round Robin
↘
B

Current SHIA-RAG design:
Strict single-parent hierarchy

Additional associations semantic edges ke through represent kiye jaate hain. fileciteturn14file7L550-L556

Safeguard
Depth Limit

❌ Raw document read nahi karta
❌ OCR nahi karta

❌ Raw relation extraction nahi karta
❌ Relation confidence calculate karne ka primary Layer 4-level task nahi hai

“Existing validated knowledge ko intelligently organize karna.”

parent for each concept, validates the placement, inserts the concept into the Knowledge Forest, and adds additional semantic
cross-links for better retrieval.”

Layer 5 – SHIA Core / Hierarchy Construction
You can explain it to your guide like this:
“Layer 5 is the core organization layer of the system. It receives validated KnowledgeNodes and KnowledgeEdges from Layer 4
and organizes them into a structured Knowledge Forest. For each new concept, it finds possible parent concepts, ranks them,
validates the best parent, inserts the concept into the hierarchy, and creates additional semantic cross-links between related
concepts.”

Simple Example
Suppose the new concept is Round Robin.
Candidate Parents
↓
CPU Scheduling Algorithm
CPU Scheduling
Operating Systems
↓
Rank the Candidates
↓
Validate the Best Parent
↓
Round Robin is inserted under
CPU Scheduling Algorithm
↓
Create semantic link:
Round Robin ── USES ──> Time Quantum

Main Components
CPG++ – Finds possible parent concepts.
PRE – Ranks the possible parents.
HV – Validates the hierarchy and prevents problems such as cycles.
FI – Inserts the concept into the Knowledge Forest.
CLD – Creates semantic cross-links between related concepts.

Output
A structured Knowledge Forest containing hierarchical relationships and semantic cross-links, which is then passed to Layer 6
for intelligent retrieval.

In one simple line
“Layer 5 converts validated concepts and relationships into an organized Knowledge Forest by deciding where each concept
belongs and how related concepts should be connected.”

[L284] --[L285]
[L286] ## 3. System Architecture
[L287]
[L288] ### 3.1 Overview
[L289]
[L290] SHIA-RAG is organized as an 8-layer pipeline divided into three phases:
[L291]
[L292] | Phase | Layers | Mode | Purpose |
[L293] |-------|--------|------|---------|
[L294] | Phase 1: Offline | Layers 1-5 | Batch processing | Extract knowledge from documents and build the Knowledge Forest
|
[L295] | Phase 2: Online | Layers 6-7 | Real-time | Retrieve context and generate answers for user queries |
[L296] | Phase 3: Continuous | Layer 8 | Background | Monitor, collect feedback, and evolve the Knowledge Forest |
[L297]
[L298] Additionally, Layer 0 is the foundational data model (schemas, types, database contracts) shared by all layers.
[L299]
[L300]
[L301] graph TD
[L302]
[L303]
[L304]

[L520] ### 4.3 Tree vs DAG vs Graph

blob:https://chatgpt.com/22bc3c39-b594-46a2-bdf0-c46ad675ec43

348/597

03/09/2026, 14:49

Layer Zero समझाना

[L521]
[L522] | PDF | Claim |
[L523] |-----|-------|
[L524] | All PDFs | "Knowledge Forest is acyclic (no loops)" |
[L525] | All PDFs | "Cross-Link Discovery (CLD) adds semantic associations" |
[L526]
[L527] Contradiction: Cross-links create graph cycles. The forest is only acyclic in its hierarchical edges (parent-child). Crosslinks form a separate semantic graph layer.
[L528]
[L529] Resolution: Define two distinct edge types:
[L530] 1. Hierarchical edges (IS_A, PART_OF) — must be acyclic, form a forest
[L531] 2. Semantic edges (USES, RELATED_TO, CAUSES) — may form cycles, separate graph layer
[L532]
[L533] > [!IMPORTANT]
[L534] > Single-Parent Constraint: SHIA-RAG enforces strict single-parent trees for hierarchical edges. Each node has at
most one parent in the hierarchy. DAG support (multiple parents) is deferred to future work. This simplifies:
[L535] > - Precedence constraints in Tree Knapsack: $x_i \leq x_{\text{parent}(i)}$ is unambiguous
[L536] > - Confidence propagation: single parent path, no need for multi-parent averaging
[L537] > - Cycle detection: simple ancestor traversal
[L538] >
[L539] > Multiple semantic associations are handled via SEMANTIC edges (cross-links), which are unrestricted.

[L552] ### Novelty 3: Multi-Objective Hierarchy Energy Minimization
[L553]
[L554] What exists: TreeRAG and RAPTOR use simple clustering. GraphRAG uses flat triple extraction.
[L555]
[L556] What SHIA-RAG proposes: Hierarchy construction as a formal energy minimization problem:
[L557]
[L558] $$J(\mathcal{F}) = \sum_{(P_i, N_i)} \left[ \lambda_1 \cdot L_{\text{sem}}(P_i, N_i) + \lambda_2 \cdot L_{\text{depth}}
(N_i) + \lambda_3 \cdot L_{\text{conf}}(P_i, N_i) + \lambda_4 \cdot L_{\text{onto}}(P_i, N_i) \right]$$
[L559]
[L560] Where:
[L561] - $L_{\text{sem}}$ = semantic distance loss (1 - cosine similarity)
[L562] - $L_{\text{depth}}$ = depth regularization (penalizes too-deep or too-shallow trees)
[L563] - $L_{\text{conf}}$ = confidence loss (low-confidence placements increase energy)

blob:https://chatgpt.com/22bc3c39-b594-46a2-bdf0-c46ad675ec43

349/597

03/09/2026, 14:49

Layer Zero समझाना

[L564] - $L_{\text{onto}}$ = ontological consistency loss (parent should be more general)
[L565]
[L566] Why novel: No RAG paper has formalized hierarchy construction as a multi-objective optimization problem for
hierarchy induction in RAG. The formulation enables principled trade-offs between semantic fit, structural balance,
confidence, and ontological consistency.
[L567]
[L568] > [!NOTE]
[L569] > The $L_{\text{onto}}$ term uses a sigmoid relaxation $\sigma(\text{type\_score}(P) - \text{type\_score}(N))$ instead
of a non-differentiable indicator function. See Section 8.1 for the corrected formulation.
[L570]
[L571] --[L572]
[L573] ### Novelty 4: Adaptive Depth Traversal via Query Complexity Classification
[L574]
[L575] What exists: All RAG systems retrieve a fixed number of chunks/nodes regardless of query complexity.
[L576]
[L577] What SHIA-RAG proposes: A query complexity classifier that dynamically adjusts traversal depth:
[L578]
[L579] | Query Type | Example | Traversal Strategy |
[L580] |------------|---------|-------------------|
[L581] | DEFINITION | "What is OSPF?" | Shallow: Target node + parent only (depth=1) |
[L582] | COMPARISON | "Compare OSPF vs RIP" | Medium: Multiple subtrees, sibling links (depth=2) |
[L583] | MULTI-HOP | "How does OSPF convergence affect network reliability?" | Deep: Full path traversal + cross-links
(depth=3+) |
[L584] | SYNTHESIS | "Summarize all routing protocols" | Breadth: Retrieve at root/topic level, expand selectively |
[L585]
[L586] ```python
[L587] class QueryComplexityClassifier:
[L588] def classify(self, query):
[L589] features = {
[L590] 'num_entities': count_entities(query),
[L591] 'has_comparison': any(w in query.lower() for w in ['compare', 'vs', 'difference']),
[L592] 'has_causal': any(w in query.lower() for w in ['why', 'how', 'cause', 'effect']),
[L593] 'num_hops_estimated': estimate_reasoning_hops(query),
[L594] }
[L595] # Lightweight classifier (fine-tuned BERT or rule-based)
[L596] return self.model.predict(features) # → SIMPLE | MODERATE | COMPLEX | SYNTHESIS
[L597]

[L599] """Rule-based heuristic to estimate the number of reasoning hops
[L600] required to answer a query. Returns an integer in [1, 5]."""

[L642] import time
[L643] from functools import wraps
[L644]
[L645] def retry_with_backoff(max_retries=3, base_delay=1.0, max_delay=30.0):
[L646] """Decorator for retrying failed operations with exponential backoff."""
[L647] def decorator(func):
[L648] @wraps(func)
[L649] def wrapper(*args, **kwargs):
[L650] for attempt in range(max_retries):
[L651] try:
[L652] return func(*args, **kwargs)
[L653] except (TimeoutError, ConnectionError) as e:
[L654] if attempt == max_retries - 1:

blob:https://chatgpt.com/22bc3c39-b594-46a2-bdf0-c46ad675ec43

351/597

03/09/2026, 14:49

Layer Zero समझाना

[L655] raise
[L656] delay = min(base_delay * (2 ** attempt), max_delay)
[L657] print(f"Attempt {attempt + 1} failed: {e}. Retrying in {delay}s...")
[L658] time.sleep(delay)
[L659] return wrapper
[L660] return decorator
[L661]
[L662] class ProcessingPipeline:
[L663] """Error handling for the SHIA-RAG processing pipeline."""
[L664]
[L665] def process_document(self, doc):
[L666] # Layer 1: OCR with fallback
[L667] try:
[L668] text = self.extract_text(doc)
[L669] except OCRFailure:
[L670] return {"status": "MANUAL_REVIEW_REQUIRED", "reason": "OCR_FAILED"}
[L671]
[L672] # Layer 3: LLM extraction with retry + fallback model
[L673] try:
[L674] concepts = self.llm_extract_concepts(text)
[L675] except LLMTimeout:
[L676] concepts = self.smaller_llm_extract_concepts(text) # Fallback to smaller model
[L677]
[L678] # Layer 6: Vector DB with cache fallback
[L679] try:
[L680] results = self.vector_search(query_embedding)
[L681] except VectorDBUnavailable:
[L682] results = self.cache.get_recent_results(query_hash) # Redis cache fallback
[L683]
[L684] return {"status": "SUCCESS", "concepts": concepts}

[L732] def run_migrations(db, target_version=None):

[L749] from functools import wraps
[L750]
[L751] def retry_with_backoff(max_retries=3, base_delay=1.0, max_delay=30.0):
[L752] """Decorator for retrying failed operations with exponential backoff."""
[L753] def decorator(func):
[L754] @wraps(func)
[L755] def wrapper(*args, **kwargs):
[L756] for attempt in range(max_retries):
[L757] try:
[L758] return func(*args, **kwargs)
[L759] except (TimeoutError, ConnectionError) as e:
[L760] if attempt == max_retries - 1:
[L761] raise
[L762] delay = min(base_delay * (2 ** attempt), max_delay)
[L763] print(f"Attempt {attempt + 1} failed: {e}. Retrying in {delay}s...")
[L764] time.sleep(delay)
[L765] return wrapper
[L766] return decorator
[L767]
[L768] class ProcessingPipeline:
[L769] """Error handling for the SHIA-RAG processing pipeline."""
[L770]
[L771] def process_document(self, doc):
[L772] # Layer 1: OCR with fallback
[L773] try:
[L774] text = self.extract_text(doc)
[L775] except OCRFailure:
[L776] return {"status": "MANUAL_REVIEW_REQUIRED", "reason": "OCR_FAILED"}
[L777]
[L778] # Layer 3: LLM extraction with retry + fallback model
[L779] try:
[L780] concepts = self.llm_extract_concepts(text)
[L781] except LLMTimeout:
[L782] concepts = self.smaller_llm_extract_concepts(text) # Fallback to smaller model
[L783]
[L784] # Layer 6: Vector DB with cache fallback
[L785] try:
[L786] results = self.vector_search(query_embedding)
[L787] except VectorDBUnavailable:
[L788] results = self.cache.get_recent_results(query_hash) # Redis cache fallback
[L789]
[L790] return {"status": "SUCCESS", "concepts": concepts}

[L17] | No cross-document fusion | Chunks from different documents are independent | Cannot merge knowledge from

[L18]
[L19] ### 1.2 Proposed Solution: SHIA-RAG
[L20]
[L21] SHIA-RAG (Semantic Hierarchy Induction Architecture for Retrieval-Augmented Generation) addresses all five
limitations by replacing flat text chunks with a structured Knowledge Forest:
[L22]
[L23]

blob:https://chatgpt.com/22bc3c39-b594-46a2-bdf0-c46ad675ec43

355/597

03/09/2026, 14:49

[L24] Traditional RAG:
[L25] SHIA-RAG:

Layer Zero समझाना

Document → [Chunk₁, Chunk₂, ..., Chunkₙ] → Top-k → LLM
Document → Knowledge Forest (concepts + relations) → Adaptive Traversal → LLM

[L26]

[L27]
[L28] The system:
[L29] 1. Extracts knowledge — concepts, definitions, relations, and evidence from raw documents
[L30] 2. Builds a Knowledge Forest — a hierarchy of semantically linked concept nodes organized as rooted trees
[L31] 3. Retrieves knowledge nodes — by traversing the hierarchy (parents, children, cross-links) with adaptive depth
[L32] 4. Selects context optimally — using a Tree Knapsack algorithm that respects hierarchical precedence constraints
[L33] 5. Generates verified answers — with claim-level evidence verification and citation binding
[L34] 6. Learns from feedback — a self-evolution loop that updates edge weights based on retrieval success/failure
[L35]
[L36] > Key Insight: Humans organize knowledge by topics and subtopics (e.g., "Computer Science → Operating Systems →
Scheduling → Round Robin"), not by arbitrary text windows. SHIA-RAG mirrors this natural organization for AI retrieval.
[L37]
[L38] ### 1.3 Objectives
[L39]
[L40] 1. Design a complete 8-layer architecture for hierarchical RAG
[L41] 2. Define algorithms for automated hierarchy induction (CPG++, PRE, HV, FI, CLD)
[L42] 3. Implement a self-evolving feedback loop that improves retrieval quality over time
[L43] 4. Create a context selection algorithm that respects hierarchical constraints (Tree Knapsack)
[L44] 5. Develop an evaluation framework (SHEF) specifically for hierarchical RAG quality
[L45] 6. Provide a fully implementable specification with schemas, pseudocode, and deployment plans

[L323] ### 2.1 Related Work
[L324]
[L325] #### 2.1.1 Flat-Chunk RAG Systems

Citation Marker: fileciteturn18file5
[L326] metadata:
[L327] query_result_index: 5
[L328] file_id: file_00000000dcc082119f935683a5e13eed
[L329] version_id: 1

[L331] mime_type: text/markdown

[L333] score: 0.02761904761904762
[L334] document_chunk_id: file_00000000dcc082119f935683a5e13eed--1--2
[L335] snippet:
[L336] | Problem | Description | Impact |
[L337] |---------|-------------|--------|
[L338] | Broken semantic continuity | Fixed-size splits cut across paragraphs, definitions, and logical units | LLM receives
incomplete or incoherent context |
[L339] | Duplicate/fragmented information | The same concept may appear in multiple chunks with slight variations | Token
budget wasted on redundancy |
[L340] | Fixed granularity | All chunks are the same size regardless of content complexity | Cannot retrieve at different levels
of abstraction |
[L341] | Weak multi-hop reasoning | No explicit connections between chunks | Cannot follow reasoning chains (e.g., A → B →
C) |
[L342] | No cross-document fusion | Chunks from different documents are independent | Cannot merge knowledge from
multiple sources |
[L343]
[L344] ### 1.2 Proposed Solution: SHIA-RAG
[L345]
[L346] SHIA-RAG (Semantic Hierarchy Induction Architecture for Retrieval-Augmented Generation) addresses all five
limitations by replacing flat text chunks with a structured Knowledge Forest:
[L347]
[L348]
[L349] Traditional RAG:
[L350] SHIA-RAG:

Document → [Chunk₁, Chunk₂, ..., Chunkₙ] → Top-k → LLM
Document → Knowledge Forest (concepts + relations) → Adaptive Traversal → LLM

[L351]

[L352]
[L353] The system:
[L354] 1. Extracts knowledge — concepts, definitions, relations, and evidence from raw documents
[L355] 2. Builds a Knowledge Forest — a hierarchy of semantically linked concept nodes organized as rooted trees

blob:https://chatgpt.com/22bc3c39-b594-46a2-bdf0-c46ad675ec43

363/597

03/09/2026, 14:49

Layer Zero समझाना

[L356] 3. Retrieves knowledge nodes — by traversing the hierarchy (parents, children, cross-links) with adaptive depth
[L357] 4. Selects context optimally — using a Tree Knapsack algorithm that respects hierarchical precedence constraints
[L358] 5. Generates verified answers — with claim-level evidence verification and citation binding
[L359] 6. Learns from feedback — a self-evolution loop that updates edge weights based on retrieval success/failure
[L360]
[L361] > Key Insight: Humans organize knowledge by topics and subtopics (e.g., "Computer Science → Operating Systems →
Scheduling → Round Robin"), not by arbitrary text windows. SHIA-RAG mirrors this natural organization for AI retrieval.
[L362]
[L363] ### 1.3 Objectives
[L364]
[L365] 1. Design a complete 8-layer architecture for hierarchical RAG
[L366] 2. Define algorithms for automated hierarchy induction (CPG++, PRE, HV, FI, CLD)
[L367] 3. Implement a self-evolving feedback loop that improves retrieval quality over time
[L368] 4. Create a context selection algorithm that respects hierarchical constraints (Tree Knapsack)
[L369] 5. Develop an evaluation framework (SHEF) specifically for hierarchical RAG quality
[L370] 6. Provide a fully implementable specification with schemas, pseudocode, and deployment plans
[L371]
[L372] ### 1.4 Contributions
[L373]
[L374] This work makes five novel contributions to the RAG literature:
[L375]
[L376] | # | Contribution | Novelty Level |
[L377] |---|-------------|---------------|
[L378] | 1 | Precedence-Constrained Tree Knapsack for context selection | Incremental (Novel Application) |
[L379] | 2 | Self-Evolving Knowledge Forest via retrieval feedback | Moderately Novel |
[L380] | 3 | Multi-Objective Energy Minimization for hierarchy induction | Moderately Novel |
[L381] | 4 | Adaptive Depth Traversal via query complexity classification | Incremental |
[L382] | 5 | SHEF — SHIA-RAG Evaluation Framework for hierarchical RAG | Incremental (Novel Combination) |
[L383]

[L401] Use relation extraction: if n appears in a relation with m outside the tree, link them.
[L402] Use knowledge bases: e.g. Wikipedia links.
[L403] These cross-links do not affect parent selection but enrich retrieval graph. They are used at query time (e.g.

[L405] Data Structure: The forest becomes a directed acyclic graph (DAG) where tree edges are “is-a/part-of” and
[L406] additional edges are “related-to.”
[L407] Data Structures and Indexing
[L408] Knowledge Node Object: Stores concept name, aliases, definition text, children list, parent
[L409] pointer(s), relation lists (with types and confidence), evidence pointers (doc IDs, sentences),
[L410] embedding vector, and a version/timestamp.
[L411] Knowledge Forest: A collection of nodes. Represented as either an adjacency list (for tree edges)
[L412] plus extra edges for related links. We can use a graph database or an in-memory graph (e.g.
[L413] NetworkX, Neo4j).

[L432] Retrieval and Context Assembly
[L433] 10. Query Analyzer
[L434] Input: Natural language user query.
[L435] Output: Query intent and candidate target concepts.
[L436] We classify the query to guide retrieval depth. For instance, detect if the query is broad (e.g. “Explain X”
[L437] suggests retrieving up the hierarchy) or specific (e.g. “Symptoms of disease Y” suggests looking at children).
[L438] We may use simple rules or a small intent classifier. We also identify key terms in the query to seed concept
[L439] matching (e.g. if query mentions “Round Robin”, we directly target that node).
[L440] 11. Semantic Retrieval Engine
[L441] Input: Query intent, key terms.
[L442] Output: Set of relevant KnowledgeNodes.
[L443] Algorithm: 1. Concept Matching: Use the vector index to find nodes similar to query. Combine with
[L444] keyword matching: find nodes whose concept or aliases appear in the query. This yields initial node(s).
[L445] 2. Hierarchical Expansion: Based on intent, decide which directions to explore in the hierarchy:
[L446] Parent Expansion: If the query is general, include some ancestors of the matched nodes.
[L447] Child/Sibling Expansion: If specific, include children and siblings of the matched node. (For
[L448] example, TagRAG-style retrieval of tag chains【10†L185-L194】 suggests siblings may hold related
[L449] knowledge.)
[L450] Cross-links: Also follow CLD-related edges to capture semantically linked concepts (like LeanRAG’s

[L12] class RetrievalResult:
[L13] """Output of Layer 6 — input to Layer 7."""
[L14] selected_nodes: list # Nodes selected by Tree Knapsack
[L15] context_text: str # Assembled context string
[L16] traversal_path_edges: list # Edges traversed (for Layer 8 feedback)
[L17] query_complexity: str # SIMPLE, MODERATE, COMPLEX
[L18] query_intent: str # DEFINITION, COMPARISON, etc.
[L19] seed_node_ids: list # Initial seed nodes from vector search
[L20] token_count: int # Estimated tokens in context
[L21]
[L22] class RetrievalEngine:
[L23] def __init__(self, forest, vector_index, cache_manager, config):
[L24] self.forest = forest
[L25] self.vector_index = vector_index
[L26] self.cache = cache_manager # Redis cache integration
[L27] self.config = config
[L28] self.seed_k = config.get('seed_k', 5) # Default: 5 seed nodes
[L29]
[L30] def retrieve(self, query) -> RetrievalResult:

[L31] # Step 0: Cache check
[L32] cache_key = hash_query(query)
[L33] cached = self.cache.get_query_result(cache_key)
[L34] if cached:
[L35] return cached
[L36]
[L37] # Step 1: Analyze query
[L38] intent = detect_intent(query) # DEFINITION, COMPARISON, WHY, HOW, SYNTHESIS
[L39] complexity = classify_complexity(intent) # Rule-based mapping
[L40]
[L41] # Step 2: Embed and find seed nodes
[L42] query_emb = embed_query(query) # Asymmetric embedding model
[L43] seed_nodes = self.vector_index.search(query_emb, k=self.seed_k)
[L44]
[L45] # Step 3: Adaptive traversal depth (NOVELTY 4)
[L46] depth_config = {
[L47] 'SIMPLE': {'max_depth': 1, 'include_parents': True, 'include_children': False, 'include_crosslinks': False},
[L48] 'MODERATE': {'max_depth': 2, 'include_parents': True, 'include_children': True, 'include_crosslinks': False},
[L49] 'COMPLEX': {'max_depth': 3, 'include_parents': True, 'include_children': True, 'include_crosslinks': True},
[L50] }
[L51] traversal = depth_config[complexity]
[L52]
[L53] # Step 4: Traverse forest from all seeds
[L54] candidate_nodes = set()
[L55] for seed in seed_nodes:
[L56] candidate_nodes |= self.traverse(seed, traversal)
[L57]
[L58] # Step 5: Tree Knapsack selection — per-tree, then merge (NOVELTY 1)
[L59] selected = self.multi_tree_knapsack(
[L60] candidate_nodes,
[L61] budget=self.config.token_budget
[L62] )
[L63]
[L64] # Step 6: Assemble context in semantic order
[L65] context_text = self.assemble_context(selected, intent)
[L66]
[L67] # Build result with traversal path for Layer 8 feedback
[L68] result = RetrievalResult(

[L343] def retrieve(self, query) -> RetrievalResult:
[L344] # Step 0: Cache check
[L345] cache_key = hash_query(query)
[L346] cached = self.cache.get_query_result(cache_key)
[L347] if cached:
[L348] return cached
[L349]
[L350] # Step 1: Analyze query
[L351] intent = detect_intent(query) # DEFINITION, COMPARISON, WHY, HOW, SYNTHESIS
[L352] complexity = classify_complexity(intent) # Rule-based mapping
[L353]
[L354] # Step 2: Embed and find seed nodes
[L355] query_emb = embed_query(query) # Asymmetric embedding model
[L356] seed_nodes = self.vector_index.search(query_emb, k=self.seed_k)
[L357]
[L358] # Step 3: Adaptive traversal depth (NOVELTY 4)
[L359] depth_config = {
[L360] 'SIMPLE': {'max_depth': 1, 'include_parents': True, 'include_children': False, 'include_crosslinks': False},
[L361] 'MODERATE': {'max_depth': 2, 'include_parents': True, 'include_children': True, 'include_crosslinks': False},
[L362] 'COMPLEX': {'max_depth': 3, 'include_parents': True, 'include_children': True, 'include_crosslinks': True},
[L363] }
[L364] traversal = depth_config[complexity]
[L365]
[L366] # Step 4: Traverse forest from all seeds
[L367] candidate_nodes = set()
[L368] for seed in seed_nodes:
[L369] candidate_nodes |= self.traverse(seed, traversal)
[L370]
[L371] # Step 5: Tree Knapsack selection — per-tree, then merge (NOVELTY 1)
[L372] selected = self.multi_tree_knapsack(
[L373] candidate_nodes,
[L374] budget=self.config.token_budget
[L375] )

[L592] ## 13. Conclusion & Future Work
[L593]
[L594] ### 13.1 Summary
[L595]
[L596] This report presents SHIA-RAG, a novel 8-layer Retrieval-Augmented Generation system that replaces flat text chunks
with a dynamically constructed Knowledge Forest. The system introduces five novel contributions:
[L597]
[L598] 1. Precedence-Constrained Tree Knapsack — the first formulation of RAG context selection as a precedenceconstrained optimization problem
[L599] 2. Self-Evolving Knowledge Forest — the first closed-loop feedback mechanism that modifies RAG knowledge
structures based on retrieval success/failure
[L600] 3. Multi-Objective Energy Minimization — a formal optimization framework for automated hierarchy induction
[L601] 4. Adaptive Depth Traversal — query-complexity-aware retrieval depth adaptation
[L602] 5. SHEF Evaluation Framework — the first benchmark specifically designed for hierarchical RAG quality
[L603]
[L604] The complete system specification covers:
[L605] - 9 layers (Layer 0-8) with schemas, algorithms, pseudocode, and inter-layer data contracts
[L606] - 12 defined functions with complete implementations
[L607] - 12 relation types across 4 hierarchical and 8 semantic categories
[L608] - 8 schemas covering all data objects from document blocks to query logs
[L609] - A 6-month implementation roadmap with technology stack, folder structure, and CI/CD pipeline
[L610] - A comprehensive evaluation plan with datasets, baselines, ablation studies, and statistical significance testing
[L611]

[L673] ## 2. Literature Review
[L674]
[L675] ### 2.1 Related Work
[L676]
[L677] #### 2.1.1 Flat-Chunk RAG Systems
[L678]
[L679] The foundational RAG approach was introduced by Lewis et al. (2020), combining dense passage retrieval with seq2seq
generation. Subsequent systems — REALM (Guu et al., 2020), RETRO (Borgeaud et al., 2022), Atlas (Izacard et al., 2023), and
Self-RAG (Asai et al., 2024) — improved retrieval quality, generation faithfulness, and self-reflection, but all operate on flat
text chunks with no structural awareness.
[L680]
[L681] #### 2.1.2 Structured RAG Systems
[L682]
[L683] Recent work has begun exploring structured retrieval:
[L684]
[L685] | System | Approach | Key Limitation |
[L686] |--------|----------|----------------|
[L687] | RAPTOR (Sarthi et al., 2024) | Recursive abstractive processing — clusters chunks and generates summaries at
multiple levels | Top-down summaries only; no concept-level extraction or entity resolution |
[L688] | GraphRAG (Edge et al., 2024) | Builds a knowledge graph from text, retrieves subgraphs | No hierarchy; flat graph
structure; no self-evolution |
[L689] | TreeRAG (Concept) | Organizes documents into topic trees for retrieval | No formal hierarchy induction algorithm;
manual tree construction |
[L690] | HiChunk (LlamaIndex) | Hierarchical chunking with parent-child relationships between chunks | Chunks are still text
fragments, not semantic concepts |
[L691]
[L692] #### 2.1.3 Knowledge Graph Construction
[L693]
[L694] Ontology learning and taxonomy induction have a rich history in NLP:

blob:https://chatgpt.com/22bc3c39-b594-46a2-bdf0-c46ad675ec43

385/597

03/09/2026, 14:49

Layer Zero समझाना

[L695] - Hearst patterns (Hearst, 1992) extract hypernym relations from text
[L696] - Taxonomy induction (Velardi et al., 2013; Bansal et al., 2014) builds hierarchies from web corpora
[L697] - Knowledge Graph Embedding (TransE, RotatE) learns vector representations of entities and relations
[L698]
[L699] However, none of these systems integrate hierarchy construction with RAG retrieval and self-evolution.
[L700]
[L701] ### 2.2 Research Gap

[L12] ## 9. Mathematical Framework
[L13]
[L14] ### 9.1 Hierarchy Energy (Global Objective)
[L15]
[L16] $$J(\mathcal{F}) = \sum_{(P_i, N_i) \in \mathcal{F}} E(P_i, N_i) + \alpha \cdot R(\mathcal{F})$$
[L17]
[L18] Constraints:
[L19] - $\lambda_1 + \lambda_2 + \lambda_3 + \lambda_4 = 1$
[L20] [matches 1-4 | match_lines 1686,1695,1705,1713 | shown_lines 1681-1718]
[L21] |--------|----------|----------|
[L22] | CS Education | 0.10 | Moderate depth variance acceptable |
[L23] | Medical/Clinical | 0.20 | Deeper, more balanced hierarchies preferred |
[L24] | Legal | 0.05 | Flat, wide hierarchies are natural |
[L25]
[L26] ### 9.2 Parent Ranking Score (PRE)
[L27]
[L28] $$\text{Score}(P, N) = w_1 \cdot \cos(E_P, E_N) + w_2 \cdot H(P, N) + w_3 \cdot \frac{D_{\max} - \text{depth}(P)}
{D_{\max}} + w_4 \cdot S_{\text{evi}}(P, N) + w_5 \cdot \text{Conf}(P)$$
[L29]
[L30] Where:
[L31] - $H(P, N)$ = Hypernym score (Hearst patterns + LLM fallback, returns 0.0 or 1.0)
[L32] - $S_{\text{evi}}(P, N)$ = Evidence support (co-occurrence + citation overlap)

blob:https://chatgpt.com/22bc3c39-b594-46a2-bdf0-c46ad675ec43

386/597

03/09/2026, 14:49

Layer Zero समझाना

[L33] - $w_1 = 0.30, w_2 = 0.25, w_3 = 0.15, w_4 = 0.20, w_5 = 0.10$
[L34]
[L35] ### 9.3 Tree Knapsack Formulation
[L36]
[L37] $$\max \sum_{i=1}^{n} U_i \cdot x_i \quad \text{s.t.} \quad \sum_{i=1}^{n} C_i \cdot x_i \leq B, \quad x_i \leq
x_{\text{parent}(i)} \quad \forall i$$
[L38]
[L39] Where:
[L40] - $U_i$ = utility(node_i) — quality score incorporating edge weights from self-evolution
[L41] - $C_i$ = token_cost(node_i) — estimated tokens for context representation
[L42] - $B$ = token budget (default: 4096)
[L43] - $x_i \in \{0, 1\}$ — selection variable
[L44]
[L45] ### 9.4 Self-Evolution Update
[L46]
[L47] After each query with feedback signal $f \in \{+1, -1\}$:
[L48]
[L49] $$w_e^{(t+1)} = w_e^{(t)} \cdot \exp(\eta \cdot f) \quad \forall e \in \text{traversal\_path}$$
[L50]
[L51] Where $\eta = 0.02$. Edge weights are clipped to $[0.1, 10.0]$.
[L52]
[L53] ### 9.5 Answer Confidence
[L54]
[L55] $$\text{confidence} = 0.4 \cdot \frac{\text{supported claims}}{\text{total claims}} + 0.3 \cdot
\overline{\text{claim\_conf}} + 0.2 \cdot \overline{\text{node\_conf}} + 0.1 \cdot \frac{|\text{cited nodes}|}{|\text{selected
nodes}|}$$
[L56]

[L62]
[L63] Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) has emerged as the dominant paradigm for grounding Large Language Model
(LLM) outputs in external knowledge. However, current RAG systems universally rely on flat text chunking — splitting
documents into fixed-size segments and retrieving the top-k most similar chunks. This approach destroys semantic continuity,
produces fragmented context, and fails at multi-hop reasoning.
[L64]
[L65] We present SHIA-RAG (Semantic Hierarchy Induction Architecture for Retrieval-Augmented Generation), a novel 8-layer
RAG system that replaces flat chunks with a dynamically constructed Knowledge Forest — a collection of rooted trees where
each node represents a concept (with definitions, aliases, properties, and evidence) and edges encode hierarchical (IS_A,
PART_OF) and semantic (USES, CAUSES) relationships.
[L66]
[L67] SHIA-RAG introduces five novel contributions: (1) Precedence-Constrained Tree Knapsack for context selection under
token budgets, ensuring hierarchical coherence; (2) Self-Evolving Knowledge Forest with a closed-loop feedback mechanism
that modifies edge weights based on retrieval success/failure; (3) Multi-Objective Energy Minimization for automated

blob:https://chatgpt.com/22bc3c39-b594-46a2-bdf0-c46ad675ec43

387/597

03/09/2026, 14:49

Layer Zero समझाना

hierarchy induction; (4) Adaptive Depth Traversal that adjusts retrieval depth based on query complexity; and (5) SHEF (SHIARAG Evaluation Framework), to the best of our knowledge, the first benchmark specifically designed for hierarchical RAG
quality.
[L68]
[L69] The system processes raw documents through an offline pipeline (input → parsing → extraction → relation
management → hierarchy construction) and serves queries through an online pipeline (retrieval → generation with claim
verification). A continuous operations layer closes the feedback loop by updating the Knowledge Forest based on user
interactions.
[L70]
[L71] Keywords: Retrieval-Augmented Generation, Knowledge Graph, Hierarchy Induction, Tree Knapsack, Self-Evolving
Knowledge Systems, Natural Language Processing

[L205] ### 7.4 Closing the Self-Evolution Loop
[L206]
[L207] The self-evolution loop is closed through the `utility()` function in Tree Knapsack:
[L208]
[L209]

[L210] User Feedback → edge.weight update → utility() uses edge.weight →
[L211] Tree Knapsack selects differently → future retrieval improves
[L212] ```
[L213]
[L214] This means edges along paths that consistently lead to helpful answers get higher weights, making those paths more
likely to be selected in future queries.

[L216] ### 7.5 Forest Restructuring
[L217] [matches 16-18 | match_lines 1562,1566,1572 | shown_lines 1557-1577]
[L218]
[L219] ## 8. Novel Contributions
[L220]
[L221] SHIA-RAG introduces five novel contributions to the RAG literature. Each is supported by a systematic literature review
(see Section 2.3).
[L222]
[L223] ### 8.1 Novelty 1: Precedence-Constrained Tree Knapsack for Context Selection
[L224]
[L225] Existing approach: All current RAG systems use flat top-k selection or simple greedy knapsack for context packing.
[L226]
[L227] SHIA-RAG approach: A greedy approximation for the Tree Knapsack formulation where selecting a child node forces
inclusion of its parent (precedence constraint):
[L228]
[L229] $$\max \sum_{i=1}^{n} U_i \cdot x_i \quad \text{s.t.} \quad \sum_{i=1}^{n} C_i \cdot x_i \leq B, \quad x_i \leq
x_{\text{parent}(i)} \quad \forall i$$
[L230]
[L231] The implementation uses a greedy utility-density heuristic rather than exact DP, as exact solutions are computationally
prohibitive for large token budgets. The precedence-constrained formulation itself is the novelty.
[L232]
[L233] Novelty level: Incremental (Novel Application) — adaptation of the Tree Knapsack formulation from operations
research to RAG context selection.
[L234]
[L235] --[L236]

[L100] #### Multi-Tree Knapsack Selection
[L101]
[L102] For multi-seed queries, candidates may span multiple trees. The algorithm:
[L103]
[L104] 1. **Group** candidates by tree root
[L105] 2. **Allocate** token budget proportionally to each tree
[L106] 3. **Run** Tree Knapsack on each tree independently
[L107] 4. **Merge** results and trim to total budget
[L108]
[L109]

python
[L110] def multi_tree_knapsack(self, candidate_nodes, budget):
[L111] tree_groups = {}
[L112] for node in candidate_nodes:
[L113] root = self.forest.find_root(node)
[L114] tree_groups.setdefault(root.id, []).append(node)
[L115]
[L116] all_selected = []
[L117] for root_id, nodes in tree_groups.items():
[L118] tree_budget = int(budget len(nodes) / max(len(candidate_nodes), 1))
[L119] _, selected = tree_knapsack(self.forest.get_node(root_id), tree_budget, self.forest)
[L120] all_selected.extend([n for n in selected if n in nodes])
[L121]
[L122] # Final trim to total budget
[L123] all_selected.sort(key=lambda n: utility(n, self.forest), reverse=True)
[L124] final, total_tokens = [], 0
[L125] for node in all_selected:
[L126] cost = token_cost(node)
[L127] if total_tokens + cost <= budget:
[L128] final.append(node)
[L129] total_tokens += cost
[L130] return final

Is layer ko samajhna bahut important hai, kyunki Layer 5 tak system ne knowledge ko organize karke Knowledge Forest
bana diya tha. Ab Layer 6 ka kaam hai:
User ke question ke according Knowledge Forest ke andar se exactly relevant knowledge ko intelligently retrieve karna.

Layer 6 is the online retrieval stage: it analyzes the query, finds seed nodes, traverses the Knowledge Forest with adaptive
depth, selects context under a token budget, and sends a RetrievalResult to Layer 7. fileciteturn21file0L19-L25

Layer 6 — Retrieval Engine
1. Sabse pehle ek line mein samjho
Layer 5:
Build the Knowledge Forest
Layer 6:
Search and intelligently navigate the Knowledge Forest
according to the user's query

Simple analogy:
Layer 5 builds the library and arranges all books properly. Layer 6 acts like an intelligent librarian who understands your
question, finds the right section, explores only the necessary connected knowledge, and gives the most useful information
within a limited space.

22. Normal Knapsack aur Tree Knapsack mein difference
Normal Knapsack
Normal rule:
Select item independently

Example:
Laptop ✓
Phone ✓
Tablet ✗

Har item independent hai.

Tree Knapsack
Hierarchy mein nodes independent nahi hote.
Example:
CPU Scheduling Algorithm
│
▼
Round Robin

Agar:
Round Robin

select karte ho, hierarchy coherence ke liye parent context bhi required ho sakta hai.
Mathematically:
Child selected
↓
Parent must also be selected

Source formula expresses this precedence rule as:
x(child) ≤ x(parent)

fileciteturn20file1L35-L43

│

Instead of randomly selecting disconnected nodes.

24. Node Utility kaise calculate hoti hai?
Source utility function ke according:
Utility
=
Node Confidence
× Edge Weight
× Evidence Richness
× Cost Efficiency

Conceptually:

1. Node Confidence
High confidence → More useful

2. Edge Weight
Previous retrieval feedback se edge weight influence ho sakta hai.
Good retrieval path
↓
Higher edge weight
↓
More likely useful in future

3. Evidence Richness
More evidence
↓
Higher utility

4. Token Cost Efficiency
Useful information
÷
Token cost

Source utility pseudocode combines these signals directly. fileciteturn21file0L133-L149

40. Sabse important one-line understanding
“Layer 6 is the intelligent retrieval layer of SHIA-RAG. It understands the user's query, finds relevant seed concepts, adaptively
traverses the Knowledge Forest based on query complexity, selects the most useful connected knowledge within the token
budget using Tree Knapsack, and sends the structured context to Layer 7 for answer generation.”

Ek simple analogy
Layer 5 built and organized the library. Layer 6 is the intelligent librarian who understands the question, finds the right
starting books, explores only the necessary connected shelves, removes unnecessary information, fits the best knowledge
within the available space, and gives that context to Layer 7.

Layer 6 – Retrieval Engine
You can explain it to your guide like this:
“Layer 6 is the intelligent retrieval layer of SHIA-RAG. It receives the user query and retrieves the most relevant knowledge
from the Knowledge Forest created in Layer 5. Instead of simply selecting random top-k documents, it understands the query,
finds relevant starting nodes, adaptively traverses the knowledge hierarchy, and selects the best context within the available
token budget.”

Simple Example
User asks:
“Why is Time Quantum important in Round Robin?”

Layer 6:
User Query
↓
Understand Query
(Intent + Complexity)
↓
Find Seed Nodes
(Round Robin, Time Quantum)
↓
Traverse Knowledge Forest
↓
Select Best Relevant Nodes
(Tree Knapsack + Token Budget)
↓
Assemble Context
↓
RetrievalResult → Layer 7

Main Components
Query Analyzer – Understands the user's intent and query complexity.
Vector Search – Finds relevant starting nodes (seed nodes).
Adaptive Hierarchical Traversal (AHT) – Explores the Knowledge Forest based on query complexity.
Tree Knapsack – Selects the most useful knowledge within the token limit.
Context Assembly – Organizes the selected knowledge before sending it to Layer 7.

Output
A structured RetrievalResult containing the most relevant nodes and context for answer generation.

In one simple line

[L410] ### 3.2 Data Flow
[L411]
[L412]
[L413] Raw Document (PDF/DOCX/HTML)
[L414]
↓ Layer 1: Validate, detect format, extract text, OCR if needed
[L415] Normalized Text + Metadata
[L416]
↓ Layer 2: Detect layout, segment into blocks, classify types, reading order
[L417] [Page → Region → Block] hierarchy
[L418]
↓ Layer 3: Split sentences, extract concepts/definitions/relations
[L419] KnowledgeUnit objects (candidate concepts)
[L420]
↓ Layer 3: Alias resolution (merge synonyms via MinHash LSH)
[L421] KnowledgeNode objects (canonical, deduplicated)
[L422]
↓ Layer 4: Validate relations against ontology, score confidence
[L423] KnowledgeEdge objects (typed, scored)
[L424]
↓ Layer 5: CPG++ → PRE → HV → FI → CLD (hierarchy construction)
[L425] Knowledge Forest (rooted trees + cross-links)
[L426]
↓ Layer 6: Query → embed → find seeds → traverse → Tree Knapsack selection
[L427] Selected context nodes (within token budget)
[L428]
↓ Layer 7: Build prompt, invoke LLM
[L429]
↓ Layer 7: Verify claims against evidence, bind citations
[L430] Answer with citations + confidence score
[L431]
[L432]

↓ Layer 8: Log, collect feedback, update forest weights

[L494]
[L495] def retry_with_backoff(max_retries=3, base_delay=1.0, max_delay=30.0):
[L496] """Decorator for retrying failed operations with exponential backoff."""
[L497] def decorator(func):
[L498] @wraps(func)
[L499] def wrapper(*args, **kwargs):
[L500] for attempt in range(max_retries):
[L501] try:
[L502] return func(*args, **kwargs)
[L503] except (TimeoutError, ConnectionError) as e:
[L504] if attempt == max_retries - 1:
[L505] raise
[L506] delay = min(base_delay * (2 ** attempt), max_delay)
[L507] print(f"Attempt {attempt + 1} failed: {e}. Retrying in {delay}s...")
[L508] time.sleep(delay)
[L509] return wrapper
[L510] return decorator
[L511]

[L518] text = self.extract_text(doc)
[L519] except OCRFailure:
[L520] return {"status": "MANUAL_REVIEW_REQUIRED", "reason": "OCR_FAILED"}
[L521]
[L522] # Layer 3: LLM extraction with retry + fallback model
[L523] try:
[L524] concepts = self.llm_extract_concepts(text)
[L525] except LLMTimeout:
[L526] concepts = self.smaller_llm_extract_concepts(text) # Fallback to smaller model
[L527]
[L528] # Layer 6: Vector DB with cache fallback
[L529] try:
[L530] results = self.vector_search(query_embedding)
[L531] except VectorDBUnavailable:
[L532] results = self.cache.get_recent_results(query_hash) # Redis cache fallback
[L533]
[L534] return {"status": "SUCCESS", "concepts": concepts}

[L783] Data Structure: The forest becomes a directed acyclic graph (DAG) where tree edges are “is-a/part-of” and
[L784] additional edges are “related-to.”
[L785] Data Structures and Indexing
[L786] Knowledge Node Object: Stores concept name, aliases, definition text, children list, parent
[L787] pointer(s), relation lists (with types and confidence), evidence pointers (doc IDs, sentences),
[L788] embedding vector, and a version/timestamp.
[L789] Knowledge Forest: A collection of nodes. Represented as either an adjacency list (for tree edges)
[L790] plus extra edges for related links. We can use a graph database or an in-memory graph (e.g.
[L791] NetworkX, Neo4j).

[L803] 12Vector Index: We maintain an ANN index (e.g. HNSW via FAISS or Qdrant) over the node
[L804] embeddings. This supports CPG++ search and semantic neighbor queries.
[L805] Ancillary Indexes:
[L806] Entity-to-Node map: For quick lookups by name/alias.
[L807] Relation Index: If needed, a mapping from relation type to node pairs.
[L808] Metadata store: (document IDs, source text) for evidence retrieval.
[L809] All indices are updated incrementally as nodes are added.
[L810] Retrieval and Context Assembly
[L811] 10. Query Analyzer
[L812] Input: Natural language user query.
[L813] Output: Query intent and candidate target concepts.
[L814] We classify the query to guide retrieval depth. For instance, detect if the query is broad (e.g. “Explain X”
[L815] suggests retrieving up the hierarchy) or specific (e.g. “Symptoms of disease Y” suggests looking at children).
[L816] We may use simple rules or a small intent classifier. We also identify key terms in the query to seed concept
[L817] matching (e.g. if query mentions “Round Robin”, we directly target that node).
[L818] 11. Semantic Retrieval Engine

blob:https://chatgpt.com/22bc3c39-b594-46a2-bdf0-c46ad675ec43

438/597

03/09/2026, 14:49

Layer Zero समझाना

[L819] Input: Query intent, key terms.
[L820] Output: Set of relevant KnowledgeNodes.
[L821] Algorithm: 1. Concept Matching: Use the vector index to find nodes similar to query. Combine with
[L822] keyword matching: find nodes whose concept or aliases appear in the query. This yields initial node(s).
[L823] 2. Hierarchical Expansion: Based on intent, decide which directions to explore in the hierarchy:
[L824] Parent Expansion: If the query is general, include some ancestors of the matched nodes.
[L825] Child/Sibling Expansion: If specific, include children and siblings of the matched node. (For
[L826] example, TagRAG-style retrieval of tag chains【10†L185-L194】 suggests siblings may hold related
[L827] knowledge.)
[L828] Cross-links: Also follow CLD-related edges to capture semantically linked concepts (like LeanRAG’s
[L829] semantic paths【29†L37-L44】).
[L830] Context Packing: Collect the text evidence for each selected node: e.g. definitions, example
[L831] sentences, and optionally a context snippet from source documents.
[L832] Budget Optimization: Solve the Retrieval Budget Optimization problem (detailed next) to pick a
[L833] subset of these nodes and their evidence that maximizes informational coverage under a token limit.
[L834] This process yields a Context Graph of nodes and edges relevant to the query.

[L53] We present SHIA-RAG (Semantic Hierarchy Induction Architecture for Retrieval-Augmented Generation), a novel 8-layer
RAG system that replaces flat chunks with a dynamically constructed Knowledge Forest — a collection of rooted trees where
each node represents a concept (with definitions, aliases, properties, and evidence) and edges encode hierarchical (IS_A,
PART_OF) and semantic (USES, CAUSES) relationships.
[L54]
[L55] SHIA-RAG introduces five novel contributions: (1) Precedence-Constrained Tree Knapsack for context selection under
token budgets, ensuring hierarchical coherence; (2) Self-Evolving Knowledge Forest with a closed-loop feedback mechanism
that modifies edge weights based on retrieval success/failure; (3) Multi-Objective Energy Minimization for automated
hierarchy induction; (4) Adaptive Depth Traversal that adjusts retrieval depth based on query complexity; and (5) SHEF (SHIARAG Evaluation Framework), to the best of our knowledge, the first benchmark specifically designed for hierarchical RAG
quality.

[L152] - Edge weight updates use a dampened learning rate (η=0.02, small increments)

issue, not retrieval issue)

[L156] ### 7.3 Self-Evolution Update Rule
[L157]
[L158] After each query with feedback signal $f \in \{+1, -1\}$:
[L159]
[L160] $$w_e^{(t+1)} = w_e^{(t)} \cdot \exp(\eta \cdot f) \quad \forall e \in \text{traversal\_path}$$
[L161]
[L162] Where $\eta = 0.02$. Edge weights are clipped to $[0.1, 10.0]$.
[L163]
[L164]
[L165] import math
[L166] import random
[L167]
[L168] ETA = 0.02
[L169] WEIGHT_MIN, WEIGHT_MAX = 0.1, 10.0
[L170] RESTRUCTURE_THRESHOLD = 0.3
[L171] EPSILON = 0.1 # ε-greedy exploration rate
[L172]
[L173] def update_forest_from_feedback(selected_nodes, user_feedback, forest):
[L174]
[L175]
[L176]

f = +1 if user_feedback == "HELPFUL" else -1
path_edges = get_traversal_path_edges(selected_nodes, forest)

[L177]
[L178]

for edge in path_edges:
edge.weight = edge.weight * math.exp(ETA * f)

[L179]
[L180]
[L181]

edge.weight = max(WEIGHT_MIN, min(edge.weight, WEIGHT_MAX))
edge.access_count += 1

[L182]
[L183]

if f == -1 and edge.weight < RESTRUCTURE_THRESHOLD:
flag_for_restructure(edge, forest)

[L184]
[L185]
[L186]
[L187]
[L188]

if forest.total_queries % 100 == 0:
rebalance_forest(forest)
forest.total_queries += 1

positive feedback because the LLM produces a convincing-looking answer), retrieval includes ε-greedy exploration:

Layer 7 ka kaam: us retrieved knowledge se grounded answer generate karna, claims verify karna, citations bind karna,

File ke according Layer 7 ka official flow hai: Prompt Assembly → LLM → Claim Verification → Citation Binding → Answer
Confidence. fileciteturn25file0L13-L17

1. Layer 7 ko ek line mein samjho
Layer 7 receives the RetrievalResult from Layer 6, converts the retrieved knowledge into a structured prompt, generates an
answer using an LLM, verifies every factual claim against the original evidence, attaches citations, and calculates the
confidence of the final answer. fileciteturn25file0L13-L17

Simple words mein:
Layer 6:
"What knowledge is relevant?"
↓
Layer 7:
"Use only that knowledge to generate a trustworthy answer."

2. Layer 6 aur Layer 7 mein exact difference
Ye pehle clear karna bahut important hai.
| Layer 6 – Retrieval | Layer 7 – Generation |
|---|---|
| Relevant knowledge dhundta hai | Retrieved knowledge se answer banata hai |
| Knowledge Forest traverse karta hai | LLM ko structured context deta hai |
| Tree Knapsack use karta hai | Prompt assembly karta hai |
| Best context select karta hai | Claims verify karta hai |
| RetrievalResult output deta hai | GenerationResult output deta hai |
User Query
↓
Layer 6
↓
Relevant Knowledge
↓
Layer 7
↓
Verified Answer + Citations + Confidence

Source architecture bhi Layer 6 ke selected context nodes ko Layer 7 mein prompt building and LLM invocation, followed by
claim verification and citation binding ke through answer mein convert karta hai. fileciteturn23file0L49-L56

3. Layer 7 ka exact input kya hota hai?
Input: RetrievalResult
Layer 7 directly Knowledge Forest mein search start nahi karta.

7. “Answer ONLY from provided evidence” kyu important hai?
Ye Layer 7 ka major safety mechanism hai.
Normally LLM aisa kar sakta hai:
Retrieved Context
+
LLM's Prior Knowledge
↓
Answer

Problem:
LLM apni general knowledge se extra information add kar sakta hai.

Isse hallucination ka risk badhta hai.
SHIA-RAG ke Layer 7 mein intended rule:
Retrieved Evidence
↓
Generate Answer ONLY from this
↓
No unsupported external claim

Source explicitly instructs the LLM to answer only from provided evidence and not use prior knowledge.
fileciteturn25file0L31-L45

13. Verification Status ko deeply samjho
A. SUPPORTED

"Round Robin uses a Time Quantum."

"Round Robin uses a fixed time quantum."
Similarity:
High

Result:
SUPPORTED ✓

03/09/2026, 14:49

Layer Zero समझाना

Source threshold:
Confidence > 0.7

fileciteturn25file0L53-L79

B. PARTIAL
Suppose LLM bolta hai:
"Time Quantum improves overall CPU efficiency."

But evidence sirf partially related hai.
Result:
PARTIAL

Source configuration mein average verification confidence 0.4 < score ≤ 0.7 hone par claim PARTIAL hota hai.
fileciteturn25file0L53-L79

C. UNSUPPORTED
Suppose retrieved evidence mein kahi nahi likha:
"Round Robin always gives the fastest response time."

But LLM ne ye claim bana diya.
System:
Claim
↓
Search cited evidence
↓
No support found
↓
UNSUPPORTED ✗

Source threshold mein ≤ 0.4 unsupported category mein aata hai, aur no usable evidence par confidence 0.0 return hota
hai. fileciteturn25file0L53-L79

D. CONFLICTING
Suppose do evidence items:
Evidence A:
Statement X is true.
Evidence B:
Statement X is false.

System simply ek side choose nahi karta.
Instead:
CONFLICTING

Aur final answer mein:
Both views can be presented with citations.

17. Citation binding ki zarurat kyu padi?
Simple answer:
Because we should be able to answer: “System ne ye statement kis evidence ke basis par diya?”

Without citation:
LLM says something
↓
We don't know its source

With citation:
LLM Claim
↓
NODE_ID
↓
Original Evidence
↓
Source Document

Isse answer traceable aur auditable banta hai.

Ye answer reliability ka biggest factor hai.

30%

Har individual claim kitni strongly evidence se supported hai?

Factor 3 — Average Node Confidence
Weight:
20%

24. Layer 7 mein technologies kya use ho rahi hain?
| Component | Technology / Method | Kaam |
|---|---|---|
| Prompt Assembly | Prompt Engineering | Retrieved context ko LLM instructions mein organize karna |
| Generation | Primary LLM | Answer generate karna |
| Fallback | Llama 3.1 8B | Primary model failure/fallback |
| Structured Output | JSON | Claims ko machine-readable format mein lena |
| Claim Verification | Embeddings + Cosine Similarity | Claim aur evidence compare karna |
| Citation Binding | NODE_ID Mapping | Claim ko evidence se connect karna |
| Confidence Scoring | Weighted Formula | Overall answer reliability calculate karna |
| Retry | Timeout retry | LLM timeout handle karna |
Source LLM configuration, structured JSON response, claim-verification algorithm, aur confidence formula specify karta hai.
fileciteturn25file0L19-L27 fileciteturn25file0L48-L107

Grounded LLM Generation
↓
Extract Claims

↓
Remove Unsupported Claims

Handle Conflicts

Bind Citations

Verified Answer

“Layer 7 is responsible for converting the retrieved knowledge from Layer 6 into a trustworthy final answer. It first prepares a
structured prompt using the retrieved context and then uses an LLM to generate the answer. After generation, it verifies each
factual claim against the original evidence, removes unsupported claims, attaches citations, and calculates an overall
confidence score.”

[L43]

[L45]
↓ Layer 3: Alias resolution (merge synonyms via MinHash LSH)
[L46] KnowledgeNode objects (canonical, deduplicated)
[L47]

[L48] KnowledgeEdge objects (typed, scored)
[L49]

[L51]
↓ Layer 6: Query → embed → find seeds → traverse → Tree Knapsack selection
[L52] Selected context nodes (within token budget)
[L53]
↓ Layer 7: Build prompt, invoke LLM
[L54]
↓ Layer 7: Verify claims against evidence, bind citations

[L56]

[L413] Raw Document (PDF/DOCX/HTML)
[L414]
↓ Layer 1: Validate, detect format, extract text, OCR if needed
[L415] Normalized Text + Metadata
[L416]
↓ Layer 2: Detect layout, segment into blocks, classify types, reading order
[L417] [Page → Region → Block] hierarchy
[L418]
↓ Layer 3: Split sentences, extract concepts/definitions/relations
[L419] KnowledgeUnit objects (candidate concepts)
[L420]
↓ Layer 3: Alias resolution (merge synonyms via MinHash LSH)
[L421] KnowledgeNode objects (canonical, deduplicated)
[L422]
↓ Layer 4: Validate relations against ontology, score confidence
[L423] KnowledgeEdge objects (typed, scored)
[L424]
↓ Layer 5: CPG++ → PRE → HV → FI → CLD (hierarchy construction)
[L425] Knowledge Forest (rooted trees + cross-links)
[L426]
↓ Layer 6: Query → embed → find seeds → traverse → Tree Knapsack selection
[L427] Selected context nodes (within token budget)
[L428]
↓ Layer 7: Build prompt, invoke LLM
[L429]
↓ Layer 7: Verify claims against evidence, bind citations
[L430] Answer with citations + confidence score
[L431]
↓ Layer 8: Log, collect feedback, update forest weights
[L432]

[L468] ## 13. Conclusion & Future Work
[L469]
[L470] ### 13.1 Summary
[L471]
[L472] This report presents SHIA-RAG, a novel 8-layer Retrieval-Augmented Generation system that replaces flat text chunks
with a dynamically constructed Knowledge Forest. The system introduces five novel contributions:
[L473]
[L474] 1. Precedence-Constrained Tree Knapsack — the first formulation of RAG context selection as a precedenceconstrained optimization problem
[L475] 2. Self-Evolving Knowledge Forest — the first closed-loop feedback mechanism that modifies RAG knowledge
structures based on retrieval success/failure
[L476] 3. Multi-Objective Energy Minimization — a formal optimization framework for automated hierarchy induction
[L477] 4. Adaptive Depth Traversal — query-complexity-aware retrieval depth adaptation
[L478] 5. SHEF Evaluation Framework — the first benchmark specifically designed for hierarchical RAG quality
[L479]
[L480] The complete system specification covers:
[L481] - 9 layers (Layer 0-8) with schemas, algorithms, pseudocode, and inter-layer data contracts
[L482] - 12 defined functions with complete implementations
[L483] - 12 relation types across 4 hierarchical and 8 semantic categories
[L484] - 8 schemas covering all data objects from document blocks to query logs
[L485] - A 6-month implementation roadmap with technology stack, folder structure, and CI/CD pipeline
[L486] - A comprehensive evaluation plan with datasets, baselines, ablation studies, and statistical significance testing
[L487]

[L616]
[L617]

python
[L618] import time
[L619] from functools import wraps
[L620]
[L621] def retry_with_backoff(max_retries=3, base_delay=1.0, max_delay=30.0):
[L622] """Decorator for retrying failed operations with exponential backoff."""
[L623] def decorator(func):
[L624] @wraps(func)
[L625] def wrapper(*args, **kwargs):
[L626] for attempt in range(max_retries):
[L627] try:
[L628] return func(*args, **kwargs)
[L629] except (TimeoutError, ConnectionError) as e:
[L630] if attempt == max_retries - 1:
[L631] raise
[L632] delay = min(base_delay * (2 ** attempt), max_delay)
[L633] print(f"Attempt {attempt + 1} failed: {e}. Retrying in {delay}s...")
[L634] time.sleep(delay)
[L635] return wrapper
[L636] return decorator
[L637]

[L657] except VectorDBUnavailable:
[L658] results = self.cache.get_recent_results(query_hash) # Redis cache fallback
[L659]
[L660] return {"status": "SUCCESS", "concepts": concepts}

[L25] ## 3. System Architecture
[L26]
[L27] ### 3.1 Overview
[L28]
[L29] SHIA-RAG is organized as an 8-layer pipeline divided into three phases:
[L30]
[L31] | Phase | Layers | Mode | Purpose |
[L32] |-------|--------|------|---------|
[L33] | Phase 1: Offline | Layers 1-5 | Batch processing | Extract knowledge from documents and build the Knowledge Forest |
[L34] | Phase 2: Online | Layers 6-7 | Real-time | Retrieve context and generate answers for user queries |
[L35] | Phase 3: Continuous | Layer 8 | Background | Monitor, collect feedback, and evolve the Knowledge Forest |

blob:https://chatgpt.com/22bc3c39-b594-46a2-bdf0-c46ad675ec43

487/597

03/09/2026, 14:49

Layer Zero समझाना

[L36]
[L37] Additionally, Layer 0 is the foundational data model (schemas, types, database contracts) shared by all layers.
[L38]
[L39]

[L107] ## 2. Literature Review
[L108]
[L109] ### 2.1 Related Work
[L110]
[L111] #### 2.1.1 Flat-Chunk RAG Systems
[L112]
[L113] The foundational RAG approach was introduced by Lewis et al. (2020), combining dense passage retrieval with seq2seq
generation. Subsequent systems — REALM (Guu et al., 2020), RETRO (Borgeaud et al., 2022), Atlas (Izacard et al., 2023), and
Self-RAG (Asai et al., 2024) — improved retrieval quality, generation faithfulness, and self-reflection, but all operate on flat
text chunks with no structural awareness.
[L114]
[L115] #### 2.1.2 Structured RAG Systems
[L116]
[L117] Recent work has begun exploring structured retrieval:
[L118]
[L119] | System | Approach | Key Limitation |
[L120] |--------|----------|----------------|
[L121] | RAPTOR (Sarthi et al., 2024) | Recursive abstractive processing — clusters chunks and generates summaries at
multiple levels | Top-down summaries only; no concept-level extraction or entity resolution |
[L122] | GraphRAG (Edge et al., 2024) | Builds a knowledge graph from text, retrieves subgraphs | No hierarchy; flat graph
structure; no self-evolution |
[L123] | TreeRAG (Concept) | Organizes documents into topic trees for retrieval | No formal hierarchy induction algorithm;
manual tree construction |
[L124] | HiChunk (LlamaIndex) | Hierarchical chunking with parent-child relationships between chunks | Chunks are still text
fragments, not semantic concepts |
[L125]
[L126] #### 2.1.3 Knowledge Graph Construction
[L127]

blob:https://chatgpt.com/22bc3c39-b594-46a2-bdf0-c46ad675ec43

489/597

03/09/2026, 14:49

Layer Zero समझाना

[L128] Ontology learning and taxonomy induction have a rich history in NLP:
[L129] - Hearst patterns (Hearst, 1992) extract hypernym relations from text
[L130] - Taxonomy induction (Velardi et al., 2013; Bansal et al., 2014) builds hierarchies from web corpora
[L131] - Knowledge Graph Embedding (TransE, RotatE) learns vector representations of entities and relations
[L132]
[L133] However, none of these systems integrate hierarchy construction with RAG retrieval and self-evolution.

[L146] # SHIA-RAG: Semantic Hierarchy Induction Architecture for Retrieval-Augmented Generation

[L152] --[L153]
[L154] ## Abstract
[L155]
[L156] Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) has emerged as the dominant paradigm for grounding Large Language Model
(LLM) outputs in external knowledge. However, current RAG systems universally rely on flat text chunking — splitting
documents into fixed-size segments and retrieving the top-k most similar chunks. This approach destroys semantic continuity,
produces fragmented context, and fails at multi-hop reasoning.
[L157]
[L158] We present SHIA-RAG (Semantic Hierarchy Induction Architecture for Retrieval-Augmented Generation), a novel 8layer RAG system that replaces flat chunks with a dynamically constructed Knowledge Forest — a collection of rooted trees
where each node represents a concept (with definitions, aliases, properties, and evidence) and edges encode hierarchical
(IS_A, PART_OF) and semantic (USES, CAUSES) relationships.
[L159]
[L160] SHIA-RAG introduces five novel contributions: (1) Precedence-Constrained Tree Knapsack for context selection under
token budgets, ensuring hierarchical coherence; (2) Self-Evolving Knowledge Forest with a closed-loop feedback mechanism
that modifies edge weights based on retrieval success/failure; (3) Multi-Objective Energy Minimization for automated
hierarchy induction; (4) Adaptive Depth Traversal that adjusts retrieval depth based on query complexity; and (5) SHEF (SHIARAG Evaluation Framework), to the best of our knowledge, the first benchmark specifically designed for hierarchical RAG
quality.
[L161]
[L162] The system processes raw documents through an offline pipeline (input → parsing → extraction → relation

verification). A continuous operations layer closes the feedback loop by updating the Knowledge Forest based on user
interactions.

[L355] ## 1. Introduction
[L356]
[L357] ### 1.1 Problem Statement
[L358]
[L359] Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) has become the standard approach for grounding LLM outputs in external
knowledge. The typical RAG pipeline works as follows:
[L360]
[L361] 1. Split documents into fixed-size text chunks (e.g., 512 tokens)
[L362] 2. Embed each chunk into a vector space
[L363] 3. At query time, retrieve the top-k most similar chunks
[L364] 4. Feed these chunks as context to an LLM for answer generation
[L365]
[L366] While effective for simple factoid questions, this flat-chunk approach suffers from five fundamental limitations:
[L367]
[L368] | Problem | Description | Impact |
[L369] |---------|-------------|--------|
[L370] | Broken semantic continuity | Fixed-size splits cut across paragraphs, definitions, and logical units | LLM receives
incomplete or incoherent context |
[L371] | Duplicate/fragmented information | The same concept may appear in multiple chunks with slight variations | Token
budget wasted on redundancy |
[L372] | Fixed granularity | All chunks are the same size regardless of content complexity | Cannot retrieve at different levels
of abstraction |
[L373] | Weak multi-hop reasoning | No explicit connections between chunks | Cannot follow reasoning chains (e.g., A → B →
C) |
[L374] | No cross-document fusion | Chunks from different documents are independent | Cannot merge knowledge from
multiple sources |
[L375]
[L376] ### 1.2 Proposed Solution: SHIA-RAG
[L377]

blob:https://chatgpt.com/22bc3c39-b594-46a2-bdf0-c46ad675ec43

495/597

03/09/2026, 14:49

Layer Zero समझाना

[L378] SHIA-RAG (Semantic Hierarchy Induction Architecture for Retrieval-Augmented Generation) addresses all five
limitations by replacing flat text chunks with a structured Knowledge Forest:
[L379]
[L380]
[L381] Traditional RAG:
[L382] SHIA-RAG:

Document → [Chunk₁, Chunk₂, ..., Chunkₙ] → Top-k → LLM
Document → Knowledge Forest (concepts + relations) → Adaptive Traversal → LLM

[L383]

[L384]
[L385] The system:
[L386] 1. Extracts knowledge — concepts, definitions, relations, and evidence from raw documents
[L387] 2. Builds a Knowledge Forest — a hierarchy of semantically linked concept nodes organized as rooted trees
[L388] 3. Retrieves knowledge nodes — by traversing the hierarchy (parents, children, cross-links) with adaptive depth
[L389] 4. Selects context optimally — using a Tree Knapsack algorithm that respects hierarchical precedence constraints
[L390] 5. Generates verified answers — with claim-level evidence verification and citation binding
[L391] 6. Learns from feedback — a self-evolution loop that updates edge weights based on retrieval success/failure

[L456]
[L457] | Status | Action |
[L458] |--------|--------|
[L459] | SUPPORTED | Keep as-is with citation |
[L460] | PARTIAL | Keep but mark as partially supported |

[L462] | CONFLICTING | Present both views with note |

[L465]

\overline{\text{claim\_conf}} + 0.2 \cdot \overline{\text{node\_conf}} + 0.1 \cdot \frac{|\text{cited nodes}|}{|\text{selected

[L489]
[L490] Every query processed through the system generates a structured QueryLog entry:

[L501] | Problem | Description | Impact |
[L502] |---------|-------------|--------|
[L503] | Broken semantic continuity | Fixed-size splits cut across paragraphs, definitions, and logical units | LLM receives
incomplete or incoherent context |
[L504] | Duplicate/fragmented information | The same concept may appear in multiple chunks with slight variations | Token
budget wasted on redundancy |
[L505] | Fixed granularity | All chunks are the same size regardless of content complexity | Cannot retrieve at different levels
of abstraction |
[L506] | Weak multi-hop reasoning | No explicit connections between chunks | Cannot follow reasoning chains (e.g., A → B →
C) |
[L507] | No cross-document fusion | Chunks from different documents are independent | Cannot merge knowledge from
multiple sources |
[L508]
[L509] ### 1.2 Proposed Solution: SHIA-RAG
[L510]
[L511] SHIA-RAG (Semantic Hierarchy Induction Architecture for Retrieval-Augmented Generation) addresses all five

blob:https://chatgpt.com/22bc3c39-b594-46a2-bdf0-c46ad675ec43

498/597

03/09/2026, 14:49

Layer Zero समझाना

limitations by replacing flat text chunks with a structured Knowledge Forest:
[L512]
[L513]
[L514] Traditional RAG:
[L515] SHIA-RAG:

Document → [Chunk₁, Chunk₂, ..., Chunkₙ] → Top-k → LLM
Document → Knowledge Forest (concepts + relations) → Adaptive Traversal → LLM

[L516]

[L517]
[L518] The system:
[L519] 1. Extracts knowledge — concepts, definitions, relations, and evidence from raw documents
[L520] 2. Builds a Knowledge Forest — a hierarchy of semantically linked concept nodes organized as rooted trees
[L521] 3. Retrieves knowledge nodes — by traversing the hierarchy (parents, children, cross-links) with adaptive depth
[L522] 4. Selects context optimally — using a Tree Knapsack algorithm that respects hierarchical precedence constraints
[L523] 5. Generates verified answers — with claim-level evidence verification and citation binding
[L524] 6. Learns from feedback — a self-evolution loop that updates edge weights based on retrieval success/failure
[L525]
[L526] > Key Insight: Humans organize knowledge by topics and subtopics (e.g., "Computer Science → Operating Systems →
Scheduling → Round Robin"), not by arbitrary text windows. SHIA-RAG mirrors this natural organization for AI retrieval.
[L527]
[L528] ### 1.3 Objectives
[L529]
[L530] 1. Design a complete 8-layer architecture for hierarchical RAG
[L531] 2. Define algorithms for automated hierarchy induction (CPG++, PRE, HV, FI, CLD)
[L532] 3. Implement a self-evolving feedback loop that improves retrieval quality over time
[L533] 4. Create a context selection algorithm that respects hierarchical constraints (Tree Knapsack)
[L534] 5. Develop an evaluation framework (SHEF) specifically for hierarchical RAG quality
[L535] 6. Provide a fully implementable specification with schemas, pseudocode, and deployment plans
[L536]
[L537] ### 1.4 Contributions
[L538]
[L539] This work makes five novel contributions to the RAG literature:
[L540]
[L541] | # | Contribution | Novelty Level |
[L542] |---|-------------|---------------|
[L543] | 1 | Precedence-Constrained Tree Knapsack for context selection | Incremental (Novel Application) |
[L544] | 2 | Self-Evolving Knowledge Forest via retrieval feedback | Moderately Novel |
[L545] | 3 | Multi-Objective Energy Minimization for hierarchy induction | Moderately Novel |
[L546] | 4 | Adaptive Depth Traversal via query complexity classification | Incremental |
[L547] | 5 | SHEF — SHIA-RAG Evaluation Framework for hierarchical RAG | Incremental (Novel Combination) |
[L548]

[L639]
[L640] Recent work has begun exploring structured retrieval:
[L641]
[L642] | System | Approach | Key Limitation |
[L643] |--------|----------|----------------|

[L645] | GraphRAG (Edge et al., 2024) | Builds a knowledge graph from text, retrieves subgraphs | No hierarchy; flat graph

[L646] | TreeRAG (Concept) | Organizes documents into topic trees for retrieval | No formal hierarchy induction algorithm;

[L647] | HiChunk (LlamaIndex) | Hierarchical chunking with parent-child relationships between chunks | Chunks are still text

[L649] #### 2.1.3 Knowledge Graph Construction
[L650]
[L651] Ontology learning and taxonomy induction have a rich history in NLP:
[L652] - Hearst patterns (Hearst, 1992) extract hypernym relations from text
[L653] - Taxonomy induction (Velardi et al., 2013; Bansal et al., 2014) builds hierarchies from web corpora
[L654] - Knowledge Graph Embedding (TransE, RotatE) learns vector representations of entities and relations
[L655]
[L656] However, none of these systems integrate hierarchy construction with RAG retrieval and self-evolution.

[L39] def calculate_ocr_confidence(ocr_result) -> float:
[L40] """Calculate OCR confidence from Tesseract per-word confidence scores.
[L41]
[L42] Tesseract returns per-word confidence (0-100). We:

blob:https://chatgpt.com/22bc3c39-b594-46a2-bdf0-c46ad675ec43

503/597

03/09/2026, 14:49

Layer Zero समझाना

[L43] 1. Get per-word confidences
[L44] 2. Filter out words with confidence < 10 (noise)
[L45] 3. Compute weighted average by word length (longer words = more reliable signal)
[L46] 4. Normalize to [0.0, 1.0]
[L47] """
[L48] word_data = ocr_result.get('words', [])
[L49] if not word_data:
[L50] return 0.0
[L51]
[L52] total_weight, weighted_sum = 0, 0
[L53] for word in word_data:
[L54] if word['confidence'] >= 10: # Filter noise
[L55] weight = len(word['text']) # Weight by word length
[L56] weighted_sum += word['confidence'] weight
[L57] total_weight += weight
[L58]
[L59] return (weighted_sum / max(total_weight, 1)) / 100.0

[L65] def clean_text(text: str, pages: list) -> str:
[L66] """Clean extracted text while preserving legitimate content.
[L67]
[L68] Safeguards against false header/footer removal:
[L69] 1. Identify candidate headers/footers by frequency across pages
[L70] 2. Only remove lines that appear on 60%+ of pages (true headers/footers)
[L71] 3. Never remove lines that appear on fewer than 3 pages
[L72] 4. Normalize whitespace but preserve paragraph boundaries
[L73] """
[L74] if len(pages) >= 3:
[L75] # Frequency-based header/footer detection
[L76] first_lines = [p.split('\n')[0].strip() for p in pages if p.strip()]
[L77] last_lines = [p.split('\n')[-1].strip() for p in pages if p.strip()]
[L78]
[L79] from collections import Counter
[L80] header_counts = Counter(first_lines)
[L81] footer_counts = Counter(last_lines)
[L82]
[L83] threshold = max(3, int(len(pages) 0.6)) # 60% of pages OR at least 3
[L84] headers_to_remove = {h for h, c in header_counts.items() if c >= threshold}
[L85] footers_to_remove = {f for f, c in footer_counts.items() if c >= threshold}
[L86]
[L87] lines = text.split('\n')
[L88] lines = [l for l in lines
[L89] if l.strip() not in headers_to_remove
[L90] and l.strip() not in footers_to_remove]

blob:https://chatgpt.com/22bc3c39-b594-46a2-bdf0-c46ad675ec43

504/597

03/09/2026, 14:49

Layer Zero समझाना

[L91] text = '\n'.join(lines)
[L92]
[L93] # Normalize whitespace (preserve paragraph breaks)
[L94] import re
[L95] text = re.sub(r'[ \t]+', ' ', text) # Collapse horizontal space
[L96] text = re.sub(r'\n{3,}', '\n\n', text) # Max 2 consecutive newlines
[L97] return text.strip()
